rationale: Your measured pace is only useful if you walk the same way along the wall. Keeping a steady, normal rhythm, not rushing and not stretching, means every step matches the pace you measured on the tape. Steady walking is what turns a count of steps into a fair measurement.

title: Move the counter bead for each step
instruction: Drag a bead along the counting string each time your foot lands.
rationale: Counting in your head while walking is easy to lose track of. Moving one bead for each step keeps an honest count you can check at the end. Crews use clickers or tally sheets for long counts for the same reason: a count you can see is a count you can trust.

title: Spot the mistakes in a partner's measurement
instruction: Look at your partner's notes and mark each mistake.
rationale: Pacing goes wrong in familiar ways: steps that changed size, a count that started too soon, or steps and tape units added together. Finding them in a partner's notes helps you both improve, and it trains you to check your own before you share it with the crew.

title: Choose how to turn steps into length
instruction: Choose the method that turns your step count into a length in the tape's unit.
rationale: If one pace is a known length, then many paces are that length many times over. Multiplying your step count by your pace length gives the wall's length in the tape's unit. Choosing that method, and saying why, shows you understand measuring as repeating a unit.

title: Follow the panel joins along the wall
instruction: Keep the marker on each panel join as you walk back along the wall counting panels.
rationale: The wall is made of panels that are all the same width. Counting the panels and multiplying by one panel's width gives a second answer to compare with your pacing. If the two are close, you can be confident; if not, you look for where a count went wrong.

title: Record your measurements
instruction: Write your pace length, your step count, the wall's length and your panel check, each with its unit.
rationale: Writing every number with its unit shows your working and lets anyone check it. It also shows how close your two methods came. The crew keeps records of every measurement it takes along the wall, so the next crew can compare and spot any change.

title: Compare with the class and the foreman
instruction: Add your answer to the class chart and compare it with the foreman's measurement.
rationale: Everyone's pace is different, but if everyone measured well, everyone's final length should be close. Seeing all the answers together shows the spread, and comparing with the foreman's tape shows how accurate pacing can be. That is how measurers learn to trust, and check, their methods.

title: Check in at the end of the wall
instruction: How close did your pacing get? What would you do differently next time?
rationale: The floodwall crew finishes each inspection by comparing notes at the end of the wall, so the class does the same. Each learner says how close their pacing came and one thing that made it fair. If anyone mixed steps with tape units, the group works one example together before heading back.

situation: A crew cart comes slowly along the gravel path towards the group.
instruction: Step to the side of the path, stay together and wait for the cart to pass.
missed: Nobody stepped aside, and the crew cart had to stop and wait on the path while the group kept counting.

situation: The foreman asks what unit your wall length is measured in.
instruction: Say the tape's unit, and that you turned your steps into it using your pace.
missed: You gave a bare number with no unit, and the foreman could not tell whether it meant steps or tape lengths.

explanation: You tried to climb the floodwall. Walls are not for climbing, and the crew measures height from the ground with a marked pole. Stay on the path at the foot of the wall and read the pole instead.
You counted one before your first step had landed. Count each step as your foot lands, starting with your toes on the line. Counting too soon adds a step that was never taken.
You added steps to a tape reading. They are different units, like adding apples to minutes. Turn your steps into the tape's unit first, using your measured pace, then compare.

You changed the size of your steps as you went. A pace is only a unit if it stays the same every time. Walk at your normal, steady pace from start to finish, just as you did when you measured it against the tape.

title: Find the three tools on the map
instruction: Mark the three parts of the practice map you read before looking at any colours.
rationale: Every good map carries three tools. The key tells you what each colour means, the scale bar tells you how map distance turns into real distance, and the north arrow tells you which way the map faces. Reading those first is the difference between looking at a pretty picture and actually reading a map.

title: Sit at the planning table
instruction: Take your seat at the planner's table before the practice map is unrolled.
rationale: The planner's table is where the levee district lays out its maps and talks through plans. Sitting there means everyone can see the whole map at once and point to what they mean. Planners work round a shared table for the same reason: a plan made together is understood together.

title: Put the map-reading steps in order
instruction: Read the title, read the key, find where you are, then read the colours around you.
rationale: The title tells you what the map is about, the key tells you how to read it, finding yourself anchors the map to the real world, and only then do the colours around you make sense. Reading in that order stops you jumping to a conclusion before you know what the colours mean.

title: Keep your finger on the school
instruction: Hold your finger on the school's symbol while your partner reads the colour around it.
rationale: On a busy map it is easy to lose the spot you were reading. Holding your place while a partner reads the colour against the key means you both talk about the same place. Planners pin a marker to the map in the same way, so the conversation stays on the spot that matters.

title: Turn the map to face north
instruction: Turn the map dial until the north arrow points the same way as the compass on the table.
rationale: When a map faces the same way as the real world, left on the map is left outside and routes are easier to follow. Lining the north arrow up with a compass is called setting the map. Crews set their maps before every job in the field so no one heads off the wrong way.

title: Measure the route with the scale bar
instruction: Commit when the measuring strip matches the length of the route on the scale bar.
rationale: The scale bar is a ruler for the map. Laying your strip along the route and then against the scale bar turns a map length into a real distance. Knowing the real distance lets a family judge whether a route is a short walk or needs a car, which is the kind of choice a good plan makes early.

title: Place the meeting pin on higher ground
instruction: Drag the meeting pin to a place the key shows as higher ground.
rationale: A family meeting place works best somewhere easy to reach and on higher ground. Using the key to choose it, rather than guessing, means the choice is based on the map's evidence. Planners choose staging areas and shelters in the same careful way, colour by colour.

title: Choose the route that stays on higher ground
instruction: Choose the route from school to the meeting pin that crosses the least low ground.
rationale: Two routes can be the same length but cross very different ground. Reading the colours along each route and choosing the one that stays higher is using the map as intended: to make a calm, sensible plan ahead of time. That is exactly how the planner helps crews choose their roads.

title: Spot the mistakes in a sample map reading
instruction: Look at another group's notes on the map and mark each mistake.
rationale: Map readings go wrong in familiar ways: a colour read without the key, a distance guessed instead of measured, or a map that was upside down. Finding these in someone else's notes trains the careful habits that make your own reading trustworthy.

title: Trace the route along the streets
instruction: Keep the marker on your chosen route as you trace it along the streets on the map.
rationale: Tracing the route slowly shows every turn and every change of colour along the way. You might notice a stretch that dips into low ground or a bridge you had not seen. Planners trace routes the same way before a crew sets off, so there are no surprises on the road.

title: Record your map reading
instruction: Write what the key says, your meeting place, your route and its real distance.
rationale: Written notes turn a map reading into a plan anyone can follow. Recording what the key says beside your choices shows your reasons, so a grown-up can check them. The levee district keeps notes like these with every map it uses, so plans can be shared and improved.

title: Check your plan with the planner
instruction: Show the planner your route and meeting place and ask if they would choose the same.
rationale: The planner knows the parish's roads and the map's details well. Checking your plan with someone who uses these maps every day tests your reading. If they suggest a change, it is usually because of something on the ground the map alone cannot show.

title: Check in at the planning table
instruction: What did the key help you see? How could a map like this help your family plan?
rationale: The planner closes each meeting by asking what everyone will do next, so the class closes the same way. Each learner names one thing the key showed and one way a family could use a map to plan calmly. Anyone who found the map worrying can say so, and the group talks about how planning helps.

situation: The practice map starts to roll up and the group's markers slide off.
instruction: Put the weights on the map's corners so it lies flat again.
missed: Nobody weighted the corners, and the markers slid into the wrong places as the map kept rolling up.

situation: The planner points to a colour on the map and asks what it means.
instruction: Check the key and say what that colour stands for.
missed: You guessed the colour's meaning without checking the key, and the planner had to show you the key before the group could go on.

explanation: You guessed what the colours mean. Different maps use colours differently, so the key is the only honest guide. Read the key first, then the map; a colour means exactly what the key says and nothing else.

You judged the distance by eye. Maps are drawn smaller than real life, and the scale bar tells you by how much. Measure along the route and use the scale bar, or your plan could be far longer or shorter than you think.

You said the map shows today's water. A flood map shows which ground is lower or more likely to hold water in heavy rain, so people can plan ahead. It is a planning tool, not a live picture of the streets.
You said families on higher ground need no plan. Every family benefits from a plan: roads you use may cross low ground, and neighbours may need help. The map helps everyone plan, wherever they live.

title: Find what the label tells you
instruction: Mark the three parts of a container's label a yard planner reads to sort it.
rationale: Every container carries a label that answers the questions the yard needs. Where is it going? Which ship or train takes it? How heavy is it? With those three facts from the label, the planner can decide which pile it joins and where in the stack it goes, without ever opening the doors.

title: Stand on the walkway behind the model yard
instruction: Take your place on the green walkway before the planner switches on the model crane.
rationale: On a real terminal people walk only on marked paths, away from moving machines and lifted loads. The green walkway around the model yard follows the same rule. Standing there first means you can see the whole yard and the crane can work without anyone being in its way.

title: Put the sorting steps in order
instruction: Read each label, group boxes by destination, order each group by when it leaves, then stack.
rationale: Sorting works best in layers. Reading every label first means no box is misplaced. Grouping by destination puts boxes for the same ship together. Ordering each group by when it leaves tells you which goes on top. Stacking last means the stack is right the first time and nothing has to be moved twice.

title: Hold the stop sign while the crane moves
instruction: Hold the stop sign up until the model crane has set its box down.
rationale: When a crane is lifting, a signal person keeps everyone back and watches the load. Holding the sign until the box is down shows you understand that the lift is not finished until it is on the ground. Real signal people hold their position through every lift, however many there are.

title: Choose the sorting rule
instruction: Choose the rule the yard uses to decide which pile each box joins.
rationale: A sorting rule is a question you can answer the same way for every box. Where is it going? is the yard's rule, because it keeps each ship's boxes together. Choosing a clear rule, and using it for every box, is what sorting means in maths, whether you sort shapes, numbers or containers.

title: Spot the mistakes in a sample yard
instruction: Look at another group's model yard and mark each mistake.
rationale: Yards go wrong in familiar ways: a box in the wrong destination pile, the first box to leave buried at the bottom, or a heavy box sitting on top. Spotting them in someone else's yard teaches you to check your own before the crane starts.

title: Turn the crane to the right pile
instruction: Turn the model crane's dial until its arm points at the destination pile.
rationale: The crane lifts one box at a time and must point at the right pile before it lowers. Turning it deliberately, and checking before you drop, means the box lands where the sort says. Real crane operators line up every move with care, because a box in the wrong place causes delays later.

title: Lower the box gently
instruction: Commit when the box is just above the stack, ready to be set down gently.
rationale: Setting a box down gently keeps the stack steady and protects what is inside. Stopping just above the stack and then lowering the last bit slowly is how operators land every box. In the model, a gentle landing keeps your careful sort from toppling over.

title: Place the first-to-leave box on top
instruction: Drag the box that leaves first onto the top of its stack.
rationale: The box that leaves first must be easy to reach. Putting it on top means one lift gets it out, with nothing to move. This idea, last in and first out, is used in stacks of plates, piles of homework and big container yards alike, and it saves time every single day.

title: Follow the box along the truck lane
instruction: Keep the marker on the box as the model truck carries it along the lane to the ship.
rationale: After sorting, boxes travel to the ship or the train. Following one along its lane shows why a good sort matters: the right box arrives at the right place in the right order. Yard planners watch these movements all day and adjust the plan if anything is out of place.

title: Record your sort in a table
instruction: Write each box's destination, when it leaves and its place in the stack in a table.
rationale: A table shows the whole sort at a glance and lets anyone check it. If a box is in the wrong place, the table shows it straight away. Yard planners keep a table like this for every stack, so the crane operators and truck drivers all work from the same plan.

title: Check your sort with the planner
instruction: Show your table to the yard planner and ask if they would stack it the same way.
rationale: The planner sorts real boxes every day and knows the tricks. Checking with them tests your rule and your stacking order. If they would do something differently, ask why; the answer usually teaches a new idea, like keeping a lane clear for a late arrival.

title: Check in on the walkway
instruction: What rule did you sort by? Where else could you use last in, first out?
rationale: The yard crew ends every shift by checking the stacks together, so the class ends by checking in on the walkway. Each learner names the sorting rule and one place at home or school where last in, first out helps. If anyone still sorts by colour, the group reads the labels together once more.

situation: A model truck rolls into the lane beside the walkway.
instruction: Stay on the green walkway and keep your hands out of the lane.
missed: A classmate reached into the lane, and the model truck had to stop until everyone was back on the walkway.

situation: The planner points to a stack and asks which box should be on top.
instruction: Say that the box leaving first goes on top so it comes off in one lift.
missed: You picked a box without a reason, and the planner had to explain last in, first out before the group could go on.

explanation: You put the first box to leave at the bottom. To reach it, every box on top would have to be moved first. The yard stacks in reverse order, so the box that leaves first sits on top and comes off in one lift.
You put the heaviest box on top. A stack with its weight high up is wobbly, like a tower of books with the dictionary on top. Heavy boxes go low and lighter ones higher, so the stack stays steady.
You sorted the boxes by colour. A box's colour often shows which company owns it, not where it is going. The yard sorts by destination, read from the label, so each ship gets the right boxes.
You walked under a box that was being lifted. On a real terminal nobody ever stands under a load, and the model follows the same rule. Walk around the marked path and wait for the box to be set down.

title: Find the signs of the current
instruction: Mark the three things on the water that show which way and how fast the current is moving.
rationale: You cannot see a current directly, but it leaves clues. A floating leaf drifts with it, a buoy leans and trails a ripple downstream, and swirls form where fast water meets slow. Reading those clues is the first skill a river pilot learns, long before they ever take a ship's wheel.

title: Fasten your life jacket and stay inside the rail
instruction: Fasten your life jacket and take your place inside the deck rail before the boat leaves the dock.
rationale: On a pilot boat everyone wears a life jacket, even the crew who have done it for years. The rail marks where safe footing ends. Getting both right before the boat moves means the whole trip can be about the river, and the operator never has to stop to sort out safety on the water.

title: Put the float test in order
instruction: Mark a start and finish, drop the float at the start, time it to the finish, then repeat.
rationale: Timing a float between two marks is a simple way to compare current in different places. Setting the marks first keeps the distance the same, timing from start to finish gives a fair reading, and repeating shows whether your first result was typical or just a lucky gust.

title: Hold the stopwatch steady
instruction: Hold the stopwatch button until the float crosses the finish mark.
rationale: A timing is only as good as the moment you stop it. Holding steady and watching the float, not the watch, means you stop exactly as it crosses the mark. Careful timing lets you compare the middle of the channel with the edge and trust the difference you find.

title: Turn the model boat's rudder upstream
instruction: Turn the rudder dial so the model boat points a little upstream of the far landing.
rationale: To cross a moving river and land where you mean to, you aim upstream of your target. The current then carries the boat sideways as it crosses, bringing it to the landing. Pilots do the same thing with huge ships, judging the angle from how fast the water is running that day.

title: Set the model boat's speed
instruction: Commit when the throttle reaches the setting on the operator's card.
rationale: Using the same throttle setting for each run makes the comparison fair. Then any difference in how long the boat takes is caused by the current, not the engine. A pilot also thinks about speed through the water and speed over the ground as two separate things.

title: Place the float at the outside of the bend
instruction: Drag the second float to the outside of the bend on the model river.
rationale: Water on the outside of a bend has further to go, so it runs faster and digs a deeper channel there. Timing a float on the outside and comparing it with the inside shows you the difference. Pilots use that knowledge to keep big ships in the deep water around every turn.

title: Say where the current was fastest
instruction: Choose the sentence that matches your float times.
rationale: The float that took the least time moved fastest. Linking the shortest time to the fastest water, and naming where that float was, is how you turn a list of timings into a finding about the river. Saying it clearly is the same as a pilot telling the ship's crew where the strong water is.

title: Spot what a pilot watches for
instruction: Look at the river chart and mark each thing a pilot plans around.
rationale: A river pilot knows a stretch of river so well they can picture it in fog. They plan around the bends where current runs strong, the shallows at the edges, and other ships coming the other way. Seeing these on the chart shows why a ship takes on a local pilot for this part of its journey.

title: Keep the model boat on the channel line
instruction: Keep the marker on the channel line as the current pushes the model boat sideways.
rationale: The current never stops pushing, so steering is a steady job of small corrections. Keeping the boat on the channel line teaches the feel a pilot has, adjusting a little and often rather than waiting until the ship has drifted. Calm, small corrections are what keep a ship safe in a moving river.

title: Record the float times
instruction: Write each float's place and time in a table, with the repeat beside it.
rationale: A table of places and times lets anyone check your finding and see the pattern at once. Writing the repeat beside the first try shows how steady your results were. Pilots and river crews keep careful logs of conditions too, because the river changes and yesterday's notes help today's plan.

title: Check your finding with the operator
instruction: Tell the pilot boat operator where you found the fastest water and see if they agree.
rationale: The operator has run this river many times and knows where the current is strong. Checking your finding with someone who has that experience is a good test of your method. If you agree, your floats told the truth; if not, you look for the reason together.

title: Check in at the dock
instruction: What did the floats show you? How would you explain a pilot's job to someone at home?
rationale: The pilot boat crew talks through every run once the lines are tied, so the class does the same at the dock. Each learner says where the current ran fastest and why a pilot aims upstream to cross. Anyone still thinking a boat's speed comes only from its engine can ask the operator before the group leaves.

situation: A large ship sounds its horn and the operator turns the pilot boat to give it room.
instruction: Sit down, hold the handrail and stay quiet while the operator turns.
missed: Nobody sat down, and the group was still standing and talking as the pilot boat turned sharply to give way.

situation: The operator asks how to steer to reach the far landing across the current.
instruction: Say to aim a little upstream so the current carries the boat to the landing.
missed: You said to point straight at the landing, and the operator had to show how the current would carry the boat below it.

explanation: You pointed the boat straight at the far landing. The current carries it downstream while it crosses, so it lands below the target. Aiming a little upstream lets the current bring the boat to the right place.

You said the current is the same all across the river. It runs faster in the deep middle and on the outside of a bend, and slower in the shallows and on the inside. Pilots know where the fast water is before they turn.
You leaned over the side to grab a float. Current near a hull pulls hard, and the rail is the edge of safe footing. The deckhand collects floats with a long net from inside the rail.

You said the boat's speed comes only from the engine. Over the ground, a boat's speed is its speed through the water plus or minus the current. The same engine setting is quicker going downstream and slower going up.

title: Find the water cycle around the lake
instruction: Mark the three places on the lakefront model where water is changing or moving in the cycle.
rationale: The water cycle is happening all around you. Over the lake the sun warms the water and some rises as invisible vapour. High up it cools into clouds. Rain falls and runs back into streams and the lake. Finding each part on the model helps you see the cycle as one big loop, not a list of words.

title: Put the cycle in order
instruction: Evaporation, condensation, rain, then the water gathering in the lake again.
rationale: The cycle has an order, even though it never really stops. Water evaporates, the vapour condenses into clouds, the clouds release rain, and the rain gathers in streams, lakes and underground. Putting the steps in order shows how each one leads to the next, round and round.

title: Stay on the path behind the seawall rail
instruction: Take your place on the path behind the rail before the operator lowers the sample pole.
rationale: The seawall edge is slippery and the water beside it can be deep. Standing on the path behind the rail keeps the group safe while you watch the operator take a sample with a long pole. Crews who work by water keep to safe footing the same way on every job.

title: Turn the lamp to warm the model lake
instruction: Turn the lamp dial so the model sun shines on the water in the clear box.
rationale: In the model, the lamp stands in for the sun. Warming the water gives some of it enough energy to rise as vapour. Watching drops form on the cold lid above shows condensation, and drips falling back show rain. One lamp and one box can show the whole cycle happening in front of you.

title: Cool the lid to the right point
instruction: Commit when the lid's cooling marker reaches the line where drops start to form.
rationale: Vapour turns back into drops when it touches something cold. Cooling the lid to the right point shows exactly when condensation starts. The same thing happens high in the sky, where the air is cold, which is why clouds form up there and not down by the lake.

title: Watch the drops gather on the lid
instruction: Hold your gaze on the lid until the drops grow big enough to fall.
rationale: Small drops join together into bigger ones until they are too heavy to hang on. Watching patiently shows the moment a drop falls, which is a tiny model of rain. Seeing it happen in front of you makes the idea stick better than reading it in a book.

title: Carry the sample jar to the plant model
instruction: Drag the lake sample jar to the start of the treatment plant model.
rationale: Before water reaches a tap, it goes to a treatment plant. Carrying the sample to the plant model shows that lake, river or ground water always has a cleaning journey first. That step, not the look of the water, is what makes tap water safe.

title: Spot the cleaning steps at the plant
instruction: Look at the treatment plant model and mark each step that cleans the water.
rationale: A treatment plant cleans water in stages. First bits settle out, then the water passes through layers that filter it, then a small safe amount of disinfectant kills germs. Each step does a different job, and together they make water safe. Knowing the steps shows why operators test at every stage.

title: Say why clear water needs cleaning
instruction: Choose the reason the operator still cleans water that already looks clear.
rationale: Germs are far too small to see. Water can look sparkling and still carry them. That is why looks are never enough, and why operators test water with instruments, not eyes. Saying this clearly is the safety idea the whole lesson rests on.

title: Follow the water through the pipes to the tap
instruction: Keep the marker on the flowing water as it moves from the plant to a model home's tap.
rationale: After cleaning, water travels through pipes under the streets to homes and schools. Following it all the way shows how far it goes and why the pipes must stay sealed and clean. When you turn on a tap, you are at the end of a long journey that started as rain.

title: Draw the cycle and the tap journey
instruction: Draw the water cycle as a loop and add the plant and the tap as a side path.
rationale: A drawing shows how the ideas connect: the big loop of the cycle, and the side path people add to clean water for drinking. Labelling each arrow with its word makes the drawing a summary you can use again. Scientists sketch systems like this to explain them simply.

title: Explain the journey to the operator
instruction: Show your drawing to the operator and explain one step in your own words.
rationale: The operator works with this journey every day and can tell you if you have it right. Explaining a step in your own words shows you understand it, not just remember it. The operator might add something you did not know, which is how learning keeps going.

title: Check in on the lakefront path
instruction: What part of the cycle surprised you? What will you think of next time you turn on a tap?
rationale: The operator ends every sampling round by checking the log with a colleague, so the class ends by checking in together on the path. Each learner names one step of the cycle and one reason water is cleaned. If anyone still thinks clear means safe, the group talks it through before leaving the lakefront.

situation: A gust blows spray from the lake over the rail and wets the path.
instruction: Step back to the dry part of the path and tell the teacher it is wet.
missed: Nobody stepped back, and the group stayed on the wet, slippery path right beside the rail as the spray kept coming.

situation: The operator holds up the clear lake sample and asks if it is safe to drink.
instruction: Say no, it has not been cleaned and tested yet.
missed: You said the clear water looked safe to drink, and the operator had to explain germs before the group could go on.

explanation: You said clouds are smoke. Clouds are made of tiny drops of water that formed when vapour cooled high up. That is why clouds can turn into rain, and smoke cannot.

You went to sip the lake water because it looked clear. Clear water can still carry germs you cannot see. Only water that has been cleaned and tested at a treatment plant is safe to drink, so the jars on the bench are for looking, not tasting.

You climbed down the seawall steps to reach the water. Wet steps are slippery and the edge is no place for a class. The operator fills the sample jar with a long pole from the path while everyone stays back.

You said rain is brand-new water. The same water goes round and round: it rises from lakes and the sea as vapour, falls as rain and flows back again. The water in the lake today has been round the cycle many times before.

title: Find what slows the water in the marsh
instruction: Mark the three parts of the marsh that take energy out of a wave.
rationale: A wave carries energy. When it moves over a marsh, grass stems rub against the water, shallow mud drags on the bottom of the wave, and a wide stretch of marsh gives the water a long way to travel. Each of these takes a little energy away, and together they make the wave smaller before it reaches land.

title: Put the wave-tank test in order
instruction: Run waves with no plants, measure them, add the plants, then run the same waves again.
rationale: Running the tank first with no plants gives you something to compare against, called a control. Measuring before you add the plants, then keeping the wave maker exactly the same for the second run, means the plants are the only difference. Then any change you see belongs to the plants.

title: Sit down in the boat before it moves
instruction: Take your seat and put on your life jacket before the crew lead starts the engine.
rationale: A boat in a marsh channel can turn and stop suddenly around bends and shallow spots. Sitting down low with a life jacket fastened keeps everyone steady and ready if the boat rocks. The crew does the same before every trip, because a calm start makes the whole visit calm.

title: Set the wave maker and leave it
instruction: Turn the wave maker dial to the teacher's setting and do not touch it again.
rationale: The wave maker must stay on the same setting for both runs. If the waves are different sizes each time, you cannot tell whether the plants did anything. Setting it once and leaving it is how scientists control a variable, the thing they keep the same on purpose.

title: Read the wave height at the far end
instruction: Commit when the marker sits at the top of the wave on the far ruler.
rationale: To compare the two runs, you read the wave at the same place each time, on the ruler at the land end of the tank. Reading at the top of the wave, and at eye level, makes your reading one that a classmate would agree with. Careful reading is what makes the comparison honest.

title: Hold the model plants in place
instruction: Hold the plant mat flat on the tank floor until its weights settle.
rationale: If the plant mat lifts or slides, the test changes halfway through. Holding it flat until the weights settle keeps the plants standing where you put them. Real marsh grass is held in place by its roots, which is exactly what the weights stand in for in the model.

title: Set the plant mat in the middle of the tank
instruction: Drag the plant mat to the marked strip between the wave maker and the shore.
rationale: A real marsh lies between open water and the land. Putting the plant mat in the same place in the tank means the waves must cross it to reach the model shore, just as storm waves cross a marsh. The position matters, because plants behind the shore would not slow anything.

title: Spot what the restoration crew is doing
instruction: Look across the marsh from the boat and mark each part of the crew's work.
rationale: Restoring a marsh is patient work. The crew plants young grass in rows, lays mats that stop the mud washing away, and places fences that trap sediment so the ground can build up again. Seeing each job helps you understand that a marsh can be helped to grow back, and that people do that work.

title: Say what the plants did to the waves
instruction: Choose the sentence that says what your two runs showed.
rationale: Your control run and your plant run used the same waves. If the waves were smaller at the shore with plants, the plants took energy out of them. A good conclusion says only that, with your readings as the evidence, and does not claim more than the test showed.

title: Follow a wave across the marsh strip
instruction: Keep the marker on one wave as it travels over the plants and shrinks.
rationale: Watching one wave from start to finish shows the change happening, not just the result. You see it lose height as it pushes through the stems and over the shallow floor. That picture, energy being taken away step by step, is the heart of why wetlands act like a speed bump.

title: Record both runs side by side
instruction: Write the wave height for the control run and the plant run in a two-column table.
rationale: Two columns side by side make the comparison easy to see and easy to check. Anyone reading your table can see the setting, the two readings and the one thing that changed. That is how a test result travels from your bench to someone else's, and how it can be repeated.

title: Compare with another group
instruction: Put your table next to another group's and look for the same pattern.
rationale: One test can be a fluke. If another group, with its own tank, sees waves shrink over plants too, the result is much stronger. Comparing results is how scientists build confidence, and it is why the crew shares its marsh surveys with other crews along the coast.

title: Check in before the boat heads back
instruction: What did the tank show you? What is one way people help a marsh grow back?
rationale: The restoration crew talks over each day's planting on the ride back, so the class does the same before the engine starts. Each learner says what the plants did to the waves and names one job they saw the crew doing. If anyone thinks the marsh stops all water, the group sorts that out together now.

situation: A passing work boat's wake rocks the deck and the tank sloshes.
instruction: Sit low, hold the handrail and wait for the rocking to stop.
missed: Nobody sat down, and a classmate lost their balance on the wet deck as the boat rocked from side to side.

situation: The crew lead asks which run you are comparing the plant run against.
instruction: Say that the bare-tank run is the control, with the same waves and no plants.
missed: You could not say which run was the control, and the crew lead had to explain the comparison before the group could go on.

explanation: You added plants and turned the wave maker down in the same run. With two changes you cannot tell which one made the waves smaller. A fair test changes one thing, the plants, and keeps the wave maker the same.

You said the marsh stops storm water completely. A marsh slows water and takes energy out of waves, like a speed bump slows a car. It does not stop the water, which is why a parish uses wetlands, levees and pumps together.
You pulled up a marsh plant. Every stem helps hold the mud together, and the crew planted each one by hand. Look, sketch and photograph; the plants stay where they are.

You stepped off the boat onto the marsh. Marsh mud is soft and can hold a boot fast, and trampling kills young plants. The crew plants from the boat or from mats laid down for the job, and visitors stay aboard.

title: Find where the rain goes
instruction: Mark the three places the rain passes on its way to the pump station in the model street.
rationale: Rain that lands on a roof does not vanish. It runs down the gutter, into the street drain, then along an underground pipe or an open canal to the pump station. Finding each stop on the model is how you follow the water's whole path, and it shows why a blocked drain anywhere slows everything behind it.

title: Stand behind the yellow line in the pump hall
instruction: Take your place behind the yellow line before the operator starts the demonstration.
rationale: A pump hall is a working room with big machines, and the yellow line shows where visitors stand. From behind it you can see the pumps, the panel and the operator clearly. Standing there first means the operator can concentrate on the pumps and never has to stop to move someone out of the way.

title: Put the pump start-up in order
instruction: Check the screen is clear, check the canal level, start the first pump, then watch the level fall.
rationale: Operators follow the same order every time. A clear screen lets water reach the pump, the canal level tells them whether a pump is needed, and starting one pump before the next keeps the flow steady. Watching the level afterwards proves the pump is really moving water.

title: Hold the model pump steady
instruction: Hold the model pump's switch until the water in the low tank is lifted into the high tank.
rationale: A pump does its work only while it runs. Holding the switch shows how long it takes to lift water from the low tank up to the high one. Seeing that it takes time helps you understand why a station keeps running long after the rain has stopped, until the canals are back down.

title: Say why this water needs a pump
instruction: Choose the reason the water in the low tank could not reach the high tank without the pump.
rationale: Water moves from high places to low places on its own. The low tank sits below the high tank, so the water had no way up until the pump lifted it. Saying that clearly is the big idea of the lesson, and it explains every pump station you will ever see.

title: Spot what slows the water down
instruction: Look at the street photo board and mark each thing that could block a drain.
rationale: Most drain problems start small: leaves piled on a grate, a bag caught in a gutter, grass cuttings swept into the street. Each one slows the water on its way to the pumps. Spotting them teaches you what your family can clear before a rainy day, which is one real way to help.

title: Open the canal gate a little
instruction: Turn the gate wheel so water in the model canal flows gently towards the pump.
rationale: Gates guide water to the pumps. Opening a gate slowly lets the canal fill the pump's intake without a rush that stirs up mud and litter. Operators open gates gently for the same reason, so the flow stays smooth and the screens do not clog all at once.

title: Start the pump at the right level
instruction: Commit when the canal gauge reaches the start mark on the operator's panel.
rationale: A pump that starts too early runs dry and wears out; one that starts too late lets the canal fill up. The start mark is the level the operators chose for the first pump. Reading the gauge and acting at that mark is the same careful choice a real operator makes on every rainy shift.

title: Move the rake to the screen
instruction: Drag the long rake to the screen once the model pump is switched off.
rationale: The screen is a row of bars that stops litter from reaching the pump. When it fills up, water slows down. The operator switches the pump off first, then uses a long rake from the walkway to clear it. Using the rake keeps hands far from the water and any moving part.

title: Follow the canal level as the pumps work
instruction: Keep the marker on the canal level as it rises with the rain and falls with the pumps.
rationale: During rain the canal rises, and as pumps run it falls again. The operator watches that level all shift, because it shows whether the pumps are keeping up. Following it teaches you that the job is not one switch, it is steady watching and adjusting until the rain has passed.

title: Record the rain's path and the pump test
instruction: Draw the path from roof to river and write when the model pump started and stopped.
rationale: A drawing of the water's path and a note of what the pump did turn a demonstration into something you can explain at home. Operators keep a log of every start and stop for the same reason, so the next shift can see what happened and plan for the next rain.

title: Explain the path to a classmate
instruction: Show your drawing to a classmate and trace the water's path out loud.
rationale: Explaining something out loud shows whether you really understand it. As you trace the path from roof to river, your classmate can ask where the water goes next. If you can answer each question, the idea is yours, and you can teach it to your family too.

title: Check in at the viewing window
instruction: What surprised you about where the rain goes? What could your family do to help the drains?
rationale: The operators end a shift by handing over to the next crew, so the class ends by handing over what it learned. Each learner names one step on the water's path and one thing a family can do, like clearing a grate. Anyone still puzzled about why the water needs a lift can ask the operator now.

situation: A light on the model panel shows the intake screen is filling with leaves.
instruction: Tell the operator the screen light is on and wait behind the line.
missed: Nobody spoke up, and the model screen filled until the water in the canal stopped moving towards the pump.

situation: The operator asks where the water goes after the pump lifts it.
instruction: Say that it goes up and over into the outfall canal and on to the river or the lake.
missed: You said the water just disappears, and the operator had to explain the outfall canal before the group could go on.

explanation: You reached into the intake while the model pump was running. Operators never put a hand near moving parts: they stop the pump, lock it off and use the rake. The rule is the same for a model on the bench and a real station.

You said street litter does not matter. Leaves, bottles and bags wash into the drains and pile up on the station's screens, which slows the water down. Keeping drains clear at home is one way every family helps the pumps do their job.

You switched every pump on at once. Operators start pumps one after another as the water in the canal rises, so the power supply and the canals keep up. Starting in order is steadier and leaves pumps ready if more rain comes.

You said the water would run out to the river on its own. Water only runs downhill. Where the streets sit lower than the water around them, it collects in the low places, and a pump has to lift it up and over before it can leave.

title: Find the parts of a circuit
instruction: Mark the three parts every working circuit on the bench needs.
rationale: Every circuit needs something to push the current, a path for it to flow round and something that uses the energy. On this bench that is the battery pack, the connecting wires and the bulb. Knowing the parts is what lets you find why a circuit does not work.

title: Confirm you are using the checked kit
instruction: Confirm the teacher has checked the kit and there is no mains lead on the bench.
rationale: Classroom circuits use low-voltage kits that the teacher has checked because mains electricity is dangerous. Confirming the kit, and that nothing on the bench plugs into the wall, is the first step every time and the habit that keeps a curious learner safe at home too.

title: Build the circuit in order
instruction: Battery out, wires to the bulb, then battery in, then test.
rationale: Building with the battery out means nothing can short while you work. Connecting the wires to the bulb and checking the loop before the battery goes in means the first thing to happen is the bulb lighting, not a surprise. It is the same order an electrician works in.

title: Trace the loop from one end to the other
instruction: Follow the path with your finger from the battery, round, and back.
rationale: Tracing the loop by hand finds a loose clip or a gap faster than guessing. If your finger cannot get back to where it started along wires and parts, the current cannot either, and the bulb will stay dark. Finding the break by following the loop, part by part, is the same fault-finding an electrician does.

title: Say what to do if a battery feels warm
instruction: Say what you do if a battery or wire feels warm.
rationale: A warm battery or wire is a sign that something is wrong, often a short. Disconnecting it and telling the teacher at once is the rule, and knowing it before anything warms up is what lets you act quickly. A warm wire or battery is a sign to disconnect and tell the teacher, never to carry on.

title: Spot the faults in a classmate's circuit
instruction: Look at the classmate's circuit and mark each fault.
rationale: Fault-finding is what makes circuits make sense. The usual faults are a gap in the loop, a wire straight across the battery and a bulb not seated in its holder. Finding them in someone else's circuit, with the battery out, trains the same method you will use on your own.

title: Close the switch
instruction: Turn the switch to close the gap in the loop.
rationale: A switch is simply a controlled gap in the loop. Closing it completes the circuit and the bulb lights; opening it breaks the loop and the bulb goes out. Seeing that shows why a complete loop is the one rule of every circuit. Every circuit, from a torch to a building's wiring, depends on that unbroken path.

title: Judge the brightness with two bulbs in series
instruction: Commit when you judge how bright the two bulbs in series are compared with one.
rationale: Adding a second bulb in series shares the battery's push between them, so each glows more dimly. Judging the change carefully, rather than guessing, is observation, and it sets up the comparison with parallel next. Noticing what happens to every bulb, not just one, is what makes the comparison fair.

title: Move the second bulb onto its own branch
instruction: Drag the second bulb onto a separate branch, in parallel.
rationale: In parallel, each bulb has its own branch back to the battery, so each gets the full push and glows as brightly as one alone. Moving the bulb and seeing the change is the clearest way to learn the difference between series and parallel.

title: Keep observations steady as you swap branches
instruction: Hold your attention in band as you switch between series and parallel and note each change.
rationale: Swapping between arrangements quickly makes it easy to mix up which result went with which. Steady, careful observation and noting each change as it happens keeps the comparison clean. Changing one thing at a time means you know which change made the difference.

title: Record the circuits and what you saw
instruction: Draw each circuit and note the brightness in series and in parallel.
rationale: A drawn circuit with its observation beside it is how electricians and scientists record what they built. It means anyone can rebuild it and check your observation for themselves. That is exactly how electricians leave a drawing of a circuit for the next person to work on it.

title: Disconnect and pack the kit away
instruction: Battery out first, then pack the parts in their places.
rationale: Disconnecting the battery before packing stops anything shorting in the box, and putting parts in their places means the next class finds a working kit. Finishing safely is part of the lesson, not an afterthought. Disconnecting the battery first and checking the kit is complete means it is safe and ready for the next class.

title: Check in at the end of the lesson
instruction: How did the circuits lesson go? What surprised you, and what would you test next?
rationale: Ending with a short check-in lets the teacher hear what made sense and what did not, and gives each learner a moment to name one thing they would test next. Nobody is marked here, and anyone who found the lesson hard can talk to the teacher or a trusted adult afterwards.

situation: A classmate says a wire on their circuit is getting hot.
instruction: Take the battery out straight away, do not touch the wire, and tell the teacher.
missed: Nobody took the battery out, and the wire's covering softened before the teacher saw it.

situation: The technician asks why the lesson never uses the wall socket.
instruction: Explain that mains can kill and that class circuits use checked low-voltage kits only.
missed: You said it would just make the bulb brighter, missing why it is dangerous. Next time, stop the lesson and deal with it first.

explanation: You said the first bulb uses up the current before the second. The current is the same all the way round a simple loop; what the bulbs use is energy, not the current itself. Getting this right is what makes series and parallel make sense.
You packed the kit away with the battery still connected. A connected battery in a box can short against other parts and heat up; disconnecting first is the last step of every circuits lesson.

You reached for the wall socket. Mains electricity can kill, and it is never part of a classroom circuits lesson; everything here runs from the low-voltage kit the teacher has checked. Knowing the difference between a safe kit and the mains is the most important thing this lesson teaches.

You joined the battery's two ends with a bare wire. That is a short circuit: with nothing in the loop to use the energy, the wire and battery can get hot quickly. Every circuit has a component in the loop, and a warm battery is disconnected and reported.

title: Find the warning signs in a message
instruction: Mark the three warning signs in the practice message on screen.
rationale: Scam messages often share the same signs: they rush you to act now, they come from an address that does not quite match who they claim to be, and they ask for a password or personal detail. Spotting those three signs lets you stop before you click, which is the single most useful online safety habit.

title: Know who your trusted adults are
instruction: Read the card: if something online worries you, tell a trusted adult.
rationale: Online problems are much easier to sort out with help, and nobody should face them alone. Knowing before anything happens who your trusted adults are, a parent, carer, teacher or tutor, means you know exactly where to go if something feels wrong.

title: Put the pause-and-check routine in order
instruction: Pause, check who sent it, check what it asks, then decide or ask for help.
rationale: Pausing first stops the rush that scams depend on. Checking the sender and what the message asks for reveals most tricks, and then you can decide calmly, or ask a trusted adult if you are unsure. The same routine works for messages, links and posts.

title: Hold off clicking while you check
instruction: Keep your hand off the link while you check the message.
rationale: A scam works when you click before thinking. Deliberately holding off while you check the sender and the request gives your judgement time to catch up with the message's pressure, and it costs nothing if the message turns out to be real.

title: Say how to check a claim before sharing
instruction: Say two ways to check whether a surprising post is true before sharing it.
rationale: Checking who made a post and whether trusted sources report the same thing catches most false claims. Saying how you would check, not just that you would, is the skill that stops you passing on something untrue to people who trust you.

title: Spot the problems in a practice profile
instruction: Look at the invented practice profile and mark each problem.
rationale: Profiles give away more than people realise: a school name, a home street in a photo, a public setting. Spotting them on a practice profile teaches you to check your own before strangers can.

title: Turn the privacy setting to friends only
instruction: Turn the practice profile's privacy dial from public to friends only.
rationale: A public profile can be seen by anyone, including strangers. Setting it to people you actually know limits who can see your posts and details, and checking that setting on every new account is a habit worth having for life.

title: Make the passphrase strong enough
instruction: Commit when the strength meter shows a strong passphrase.
rationale: A passphrase made of several unrelated words is long and hard to guess, yet easy for you to remember. Watching the strength meter rise as you add words shows why length matters more than a single odd symbol.

title: Move the scam message to report
instruction: Drag the scam message to the report folder instead of replying.
rationale: Reporting a scam helps the service block it for others, while replying tells the sender your account is active. Moving it to report and then deleting it is the safe way to deal with it, and showing a trusted adult is always fine too.

title: Keep a group chat kind
instruction: Keep the chat's tone in the kind band as messages come in, stepping in gently when it slips.
rationale: Group chats can turn unkind quickly, and people often go along with it. Keeping your own messages kind, and gently stepping in or telling an adult when others are unkind, is what being a good digital citizen looks like day to day.

title: Record your safety checklist
instruction: Write the checks you will use: pause, sender, request, privacy, passphrase.
rationale: A short personal checklist makes good habits automatic. Writing it in your own words helps you remember it when a real message arrives and you have only a moment to decide.

title: Share one tip with a younger learner
instruction: Pick one tip you would teach a younger learner and practise saying it.
rationale: Teaching someone else is one of the best ways to remember something yourself. Choosing one clear tip and saying it simply prepares you to help a younger brother, sister or friend stay safe too.

title: Check in at the end of the lesson
instruction: Is there anything online that worries you? Who would you tell?
rationale: The session ends with each learner describing one choice they made online today and what they would do if a message worried them. Saying who they would go to, at school or at home, is the point; the college's IT staff listen for the learners who can name a person and not just a button.

situation: On the practice chat, a new contact nobody knows asks for a photo and says to keep it secret.
instruction: Stop replying and tell the tutor straight away.
missed: The chat carried on, and the request got more pushy before anyone told an adult.

situation: The digital skills tutor asks how you would check whether a link in a message is safe.
instruction: Say you would pause, check the sender and what it asks, and ask an adult if unsure.
missed: You said you would just click and see, and the tutor showed you where that link really went.

explanation: You clicked the link in a message saying you had won a prize. Messages that rush you with prizes or threats are a common trick to steal accounts; pause, do not click, and show a trusted adult or delete it.

You used the same password for every account. If one site leaks it, every account is open; a different strong passphrase for each, kept in a safe place or a password manager a trusted adult helps you set up, keeps one leak from becoming many.

You shared a shocking post before checking it. Posts built to shock spread fast whether they are true or not; check who made it and whether trusted sources agree, and if you cannot tell, do not pass it on.

You shared where you live with someone you only know online. Personal details like your address, school or phone number stay private; people online are not always who they say they are, and a trusted adult can help if someone keeps asking.

title: Find the three roles on the transect
instruction: Mark one producer, one consumer and one decomposer on the camera feed.
rationale: Every ecosystem runs on three jobs. Producers, like the kelp, make food from sunlight; consumers, like urchins and fish, eat other living things; decomposers break down what dies and return it to the water. Finding one of each on the real transect shows that the diagram in the textbook is happening right below the boat.

title: Check your lifejacket and stay inside the rail
instruction: Check your lifejacket is fastened and take your place inside the rail by the screen.
rationale: On a boat above a dive, the deck crew's first rule for visitors is a fastened lifejacket and a place inside the rail. The divers depend on the tender crew's full attention, and a learner who stays put lets them give it, which is part of keeping the dive safe.

title: Put the survey method in order
instruction: Follow the line, identify each living thing, record it, then build the web.
rationale: A transect survey follows a fixed line so the same place can be surveyed again and compared. Identifying each living thing as the camera passes, recording it straight away, and only then building the food web from the record keeps the web based on evidence rather than on what you expected to find.

title: Hold the screen view steady on the line
instruction: Hold the camera control steady on the tape while the diver moves along it.
rationale: A survey only counts what is along the line, so the camera has to stay on the tape. Holding the view steady while the diver swims keeps the survey fair: the same strip is watched from start to end, and nothing is counted twice or missed because the camera wandered.

title: Say what happens if the urchin's predator goes
instruction: Say what could happen to the kelp if the urchins' predator disappeared, and why.
rationale: With no predator, urchins can grow in number and graze the kelp faster than it regrows. Explaining that chain, predator to urchin to kelp, is understanding the web as a system rather than a list, which is what ecology is about.

title: Spot the problems in a classmate's food web
instruction: Look at the draft food web and mark each problem.
rationale: Food webs go wrong in a few ways: an arrow pointing the wrong way, an animal the camera never showed and a missing producer at the base. Spotting them in someone else's web helps you check that your own tells the truth about the transect.

title: Turn the web card to add a link
instruction: Turn the arrow on the web card so it points from the kelp to the urchin.
rationale: The arrow in a food web shows where the energy goes, so it points from the food to the animal that eats it. Turning it the right way for one link, kelp to urchin, sets the pattern for every other link you draw.

title: Judge the visibility before counting
instruction: Commit when the visibility bar shows the water is clear enough to count.
rationale: If the water is too murky, animals are missed and the count comes out low for the wrong reason. Surveyors note the visibility before they count and write it in the record, so that a low count on a murky day is not mistaken for a real decline in the forest.

title: Place the sea star in the web
instruction: Drag the sea star card to where it belongs: an eater of urchins.
rationale: A predator that eats urchins keeps their numbers in check, and fewer urchins means more kelp survives. Placing it above the urchin in the web shows that chain, and it is the kind of link marine scientists watch when they ask why a kelp forest is thriving or thinning.

title: Follow the diver along the line
instruction: Keep the survey marker on the diver as they move along the transect.
rationale: The diver moves steadily along the tape, and the count keeps pace with them. Following at their speed, not racing ahead to the interesting bits, is what makes every stretch of the line get the same attention.

title: Record the count and the web
instruction: Write each kind seen, how many, the visibility and your food web.
rationale: A written survey can be compared with next season's, and only then can anyone say whether the forest is changing. Recording visibility with the count, and the web with its evidence, lets another scientist trust and reuse your work.

title: Hand the record to the scientist
instruction: Give your record to the marine scientist for the season's log.
rationale: A class record that joins the scientist's own adds another pair of eyes to the survey. Handing it over, complete and labelled, is how citizen science works: careful observation by many people building a picture no one person could.

title: Check in at the end of the trip
instruction: What did the camera show you that surprised you? What would you look for next time?
rationale: Back on the tender's deck, the survey ends the way a dive crew debriefs: each person names one thing they counted and one thing they would count differently. Hearing the group's answers shows the skipper who has grasped the transect line and who wants another pass along it.

situation: The tender crew raises a hand and calls that the divers are coming up.
instruction: Sit down in your place and keep clear of the side while the divers surface.
missed: Learners crowded the side, and the crew had to stop and move everyone back before helping the divers.

situation: The marine scientist points at your web and asks which way the arrow between kelp and urchin should go.
instruction: Say it points from the kelp to the urchin, because energy goes to the eater.
missed: You said from the urchin to the kelp, and the scientist had to explain the arrow again.

explanation: You drew the food-web arrow from the animal to its food. By agreement the arrow shows where the energy goes, so it points from the food to the eater: kelp to urchin, urchin to its predator. Backwards arrows make the web say the opposite of what happens.

You added animals to the count that you expected but did not see on the camera. A survey records what was observed along the line, nothing more; a count padded with guesses cannot show whether the forest is changing.

You leaned over the side of the tender to look for the divers. Learners stay inside the rail on deck, wearing their lifejackets, and the camera screen shows everything the divers see; the side is the dive team's working area.

You said taking one kind of animal out of the kelp forest would change nothing. In a food web, everything that ate it loses food and everything it ate loses a predator; one change spreads through the whole web, which is why ecologists watch every link.

title: Find the energy stores and transfers
instruction: Mark the three places on the model where energy is stored or transferred.
rationale: Following energy starts with finding where it is: in the moving air from the fan, in the turning blades and shaft, and in the electrical circuit that lights the small lamp. Naming each store and transfer before testing anything is what lets you tell the full energy story afterwards.

title: Put the energy chain in order
instruction: Moving air, turning blades, generator, electricity in the circuit.
rationale: Each link in the chain passes energy to the next: moving air pushes the blades, the turning shaft drives the generator, and the generator transfers energy into the circuit. Putting the links in order shows how the energy travels, which matters far more than memorising the words.

title: Take your place behind the barrier
instruction: Stand at the visitor point; the guide brings the model turbine to you.
rationale: The visitor barrier keeps people clear of the working area around real turbines, and the model is brought to the visitor point for exactly that reason. Starting behind the barrier is the site's rule, and a lesson at a working site always keeps the site's rules first.

title: Turn the fan to a faster setting
instruction: Turn only the fan setting up, keeping the blades the same.
rationale: Changing only the fan setting, with the same blades, is the fair test that shows more moving air means more energy transferred. Keeping everything else the same is what lets you say the fan speed made the difference. If the blade angle had changed too, you could not tell which one caused it.

title: Set the blade angle to catch the wind
instruction: Commit when the blade angle catches the moving air well — not flat to it, not edge on.
rationale: Blades flat to the wind are pushed but do not turn well; blades edge on let the air slip past. An angle in between turns the push of the air into rotation best, which is why real turbines can change their blade angle. Turning the blades lets a turbine catch more of a gentle wind and spill some of a strong one.

title: Watch the lamp as the blades turn
instruction: Keep still and watch the lamp brighten as the model's blades speed up.
rationale: Watching the lamp while the blades turn links something you can see to the energy transfer you cannot. Keeping still and watching carefully, without nudging the model, lets you see the lamp respond to the moving air, which is the evidence for the whole chain.

title: Put your result on the class board
instruction: Drag your result card onto the class results board beside everyone else's.
rationale: One group's result could be a fluke; the whole class's results together show whether the pattern is real. Putting yours on the board is how science builds confidence in a finding, and it lets the class spot any result worth repeating. Comparing results across groups shows which patterns hold up and which were chance.

title: Spot the problems in a classmate's energy story
instruction: Look at the classmate's energy story and mark each problem.
rationale: Energy stories go wrong in predictable ways: saying energy is made, forgetting wasted energy and drawing a conclusion from an unfair test. Spotting them in someone else's story makes your own explanation more careful and more complete. Finding a missing step in someone else's chain often reveals the same gap in your own.

title: Name where energy is wasted
instruction: The model hums and the shaft is slightly warm. Say where energy is being wasted.
rationale: The hum and the warm shaft are energy transferred to places we did not want: sound and heat. Naming the wasted energy completes the story and explains why no machine turns all of its input into useful output. Engineers work to reduce that waste, but they can never remove it completely.

title: Keep your notes matched to the model
instruction: Hold your notes in band with what the lamp actually does as you change settings.
rationale: It is easy to write the result you expected. Keeping notes matched to what the lamp actually does, including a result that surprised you, is the honesty that makes a science finding worth trusting and repeating. An unexpected result is a reason to test again, not a reason to change the numbers.

title: Record the energy story and the tests
instruction: Write the energy chain, the fair tests and where energy was wasted.
rationale: Recording the chain, the tests and the wasted energy gives a complete, checkable energy story. Anyone can repeat the tests from your record, and the record shows how your explanation was built from evidence. It also lets another group repeat your test and see if they find the same.

title: Tell the energy story to the class
instruction: Tell the class where the energy came from, where it went, and where some was wasted.
rationale: Telling the energy story aloud, from moving air to light and the heat and sound along the way, is the best test of whether it makes sense. Classmates who said the turbine makes energy learn most from hearing where it really comes from. Saying it in your own words is the best check that you understand it yourself.

title: Check in at the end of the lesson
instruction: How did the energy lesson go? What surprised you, and what would you test next?
rationale: Ending with a short check-in lets the teacher hear what made sense and what did not, and gives each learner a moment to name one thing they would test next. Nobody is marked here, and anyone who found the lesson hard can talk to the teacher or a trusted adult afterwards.

situation: A gust of wind tips the model turbine towards the edge of the table.
instruction: Step back from the spinning blades and tell the guide; do not grab them.
missed: Nobody told the guide, and a classmate grabbed the blades and caught a finger. Next time, stop the lesson and deal with it first.

situation: The visitor point guide asks where the lamp's energy came from.
instruction: Trace it back through the generator and blades to the moving air.
missed: You said the turbine made it, which misses where the energy came from. Next time, stop the lesson and deal with it first.

explanation: You changed the fan speed and the blades in the same test. A fair test changes one thing at a time, so you know which change made the difference to the model's output.

You walked past the visitor barrier towards the tower. The barrier keeps visitors clear of the working area around a turbine, and the model turbine is brought to the visitor point for the lesson; the lesson stays behind the barrier.

You said all of the wind's energy becomes electricity. Every real transfer wastes some energy, here as heat in the moving parts and as sound; naming the wasted energy is what makes the energy story complete and honest.

You said the turbine makes energy. Energy is never made or destroyed; the turbine transfers the energy of moving air into electrical energy, with some wasted as heat and sound. Saying where the energy came from is the whole point of the lesson.

title: Find the machines that move containers
instruction: Mark the three kinds of machines that move containers around the port.
rationale: A port moves containers with several kinds of machines. Cranes lift them off ships, yard tractors pull them around the terminal, and drayage trucks carry them out to warehouses. When these machines run on diesel, they make exhaust right where people work and nearby families live, which is why the kind of power matters.

title: Put the exhaust test in order
instruction: Clean the filter, run the diesel model, check it, then run the electric model with a clean filter.
rationale: A fair comparison starts with a clean filter each time. Running the diesel model and checking the filter shows what its exhaust leaves behind. Then a fresh filter and the electric model for the same time shows the difference, with the kind of power as the only change.

title: Stay behind the yellow line
instruction: Stand behind the yellow line on the walkway with the crew lead.
rationale: Container yards are busy places with big machines, and electric machines are so quiet you may not hear them coming. Standing behind the yellow line keeps the class clear of every moving machine. The crew lead watches the yard so the class can watch the lesson.

title: Set the run timer and leave it
instruction: Turn the timer dial to the teacher's setting for both runs.
rationale: Both models must run for the same time, or the comparison is not fair. A longer run would leave more specks on the filter no matter what. Setting the timer once for both runs keeps the time the same, so only the kind of power changes.

title: Read the specks on the filter
instruction: Commit when the marker matches the filter's colour on the grey scale.
rationale: Matching the filter against a grey scale turns what you see into a reading you can compare. A dark filter means more tiny particles, and a clean one means fewer. Scientists who watch air near ports use instruments that do the same job much more precisely.

title: Hold the filter tube steady
instruction: Hold the filter tube over the model's exhaust until the timer ends.
rationale: If the tube slips, some exhaust escapes past the filter and the reading is too low. Holding it steady catches everything the model gives off. Careful collecting is what makes a comparison honest, for a class model and for real air monitoring.

title: Park the electric tractor at the charger
instruction: Drag the model yard tractor to the charging bay on the model yard.
rationale: Electric machines recharge between jobs in a charging yard. Parking in the marked bay puts the machine where trained crew can connect it safely. Planning where machines charge is a big part of switching a port to electric equipment.

title: Spot the port's zero-emission equipment
instruction: Look across the terminal and mark each part of the clean equipment.
rationale: The Port of Oakland says its Clean Ports award pays for electric and hydrogen cargo handling equipment, drayage trucks, charging infrastructure and a battery energy storage system. Seeing each kind in the scene helps you picture what a zero-emission port looks like. A battery energy storage system is a set of large batteries that hold electricity until it is needed.

title: Say what your filters showed
instruction: Choose the sentence that says what the two runs showed.
rationale: Both models ran for the same time with clean filters. The diesel filter came out darker, and the electric filter stayed clean. A good answer says electric machines make no exhaust where they run, and it does not claim more than the two filters showed.

title: Follow the breeze from the port
instruction: Keep the marker on the smoke puff as the breeze carries it inland.
rationale: Exhaust does not stay where it is made. The breeze carries it over fences and streets to homes and schools. Following the puff shows why cleaner machines at the port help people who live nearby, not only the people who work there.

title: Record the port's plan in your own words
instruction: Write what the Port of Oakland says the award is for and what it expects.
rationale: The Port of Oakland says the Clean Ports Program awarded it three hundred twenty-two million dollars for six hundred sixty-three pieces of zero-emission equipment, and expects a cut of twenty-four thousand tons of greenhouse gas a year and a significant decrease in particulate matter. Writing it in your own words, with the source named, is how a careful reporter works.

title: Share one reason clean air matters
instruction: Tell another group one reason cleaner air near a port helps people.
rationale: Families, students and workers all breathe the air near a port. Sharing reasons helps the class see how one change at the port reaches many people. Neighbours who live near ports often ask for cleaner air for the same reasons.

title: Check in before leaving the walkway
instruction: Why do electric trucks and cranes help the air? Who breathes that air?
rationale: The crew talks over each visit before the class leaves the walkway. Each learner says why electric machines help the air and names who breathes it. If anyone thinks exhaust is only a smell, the group sorts it out now.

situation: An electric yard tractor rolls past the walkway almost without a sound.
instruction: Stop, look both ways and wait for the crew lead's signal.
missed: The class kept walking without looking, and the crew lead had to stop everyone at the crossing.

situation: The crew lead asks who helps workers learn the new equipment.
instruction: Say the Port of Oakland names the Pacific Maritime Association for skills and safety training.
missed: You could not say who helps train the crews, and the crew lead had to explain before the class could go on.

explanation: You said electric trucks are too weak for containers. Electric motors are strong, and battery and hydrogen machines are built for this work. The difference is that they make no exhaust where they run.
You said exhaust is only a bad smell. Diesel exhaust carries tiny particles that people breathe in. Less exhaust near homes and schools means cleaner air for the neighbours.
You reached for the charging cable. Chargers carry a lot of electricity and only trained crew connect them. Look at the charger from behind the line, and let the crew show how it works.
You started into the container yard. Big machines move there all the time, and electric ones are very quiet. Visitors stay behind the yellow line with the crew lead and watch from the walkway.

title: Find the parts of a fair survey
instruction: Mark the three things that make the count fair.
rationale: A fair survey follows fixed rules so anyone can repeat it. The survey box marks exactly where to count, the timer sets how long to count, and the rule card says which birds count. When the place, the time and the rules stay the same, counts from different days can be compared honestly.

title: Agree on the rules before you start
instruction: Read the rule card aloud with your group before the timer starts.
rationale: Agreeing on the rules first means everyone counts the same way. If one person counts gulls and another does not, the totals cannot be added or compared. Survey leads always read the rules together at the start, because a count is only as good as its rules.

title: Put the survey steps in order
instruction: Put the steps of a fair count in order.
