rationale: A survey has a fixed order so it can be repeated. You agree on the rules, start the timer, sweep the box once from left to right, and then stop and add up. Doing it the same way every time is what lets a count from this week be compared with one from next month.

title: Hold the binoculars steady through the sweep
instruction: Hold the binoculars steady while you sweep the box slowly.
rationale: A steady sweep means each bird passes through your view once. Jerky movement makes birds jump in and out of view, and that leads to double counts. Careful, slow sweeping is the skill real surveyors practise most. Surveyors often practise sweeping on an empty stretch first, so their movement is smooth when the birds are there.

title: Focus the binoculars on the survey box
instruction: Turn the focus wheel until the birds in the survey box are sharp.
rationale: Sharp binoculars help you tell one kind of bird from another and see birds that are close together. A blurry view leads to missed birds or double counts. Setting the focus before the timer starts means your count begins cleanly.

title: Read the survey timer
instruction: Commit when the timer marker reaches the end of the counting time.
rationale: Stopping exactly when the timer ends keeps every count the same length. Counting longer would find more birds even if the shore had not changed. Reading the timer carefully is a small step that keeps the whole survey fair. Counts of different lengths cannot be compared, just like races of different lengths cannot.

title: Place the tally mark in the right column
instruction: Drag the tally for the sandpiper into the sandpiper column.
rationale: Each kind of bird has its own column on the survey sheet. Putting each tally in the right place keeps the totals correct for every kind. Survey sheets are laid out this way so that anyone can add them up and check them. A tally in the wrong column makes one kind of bird look common and another look rare.

title: Say why the count is fair
instruction: Choose the sentence that explains why your count can be compared.
rationale: Your count used the same box, the same time and the same rules as the other group. That is why the two counts can be compared. A good answer names those three things and does not claim the count shows more than it does. When the place, the time and the rules match, a difference in the count is more likely to be real.

title: Spot the kinds of shorebirds in the box
instruction: Look through the binoculars and mark each kind on the rule card.
rationale: Knowing the kinds on the rule card helps you count only what the survey asks for. A small sandpiper running at the edge, a tall egret standing still and a duck floating nearby are each counted in their own column. Telling them apart is the first skill of any bird survey.

title: Follow one bird as it moves in the box
instruction: Keep the marker on the egret as it walks across the survey box.
rationale: Following one bird shows why counting in a single sweep matters. The egret walks from one side to the other, so a careless counter might count it twice. Watching it helps you see how surveyors avoid double counts. The same idea works for counting cars, people or trees: count each one once, on one pass.

title: Record the tally totals
instruction: Write the total for each kind of bird at the bottom of its column.
rationale: Adding each column gives the totals that the survey reports. Writing them neatly lets another person check your adding. The park crew keeps these totals from every survey, so changes on the shore can be seen over time. Clear totals let the park crew see whether more or fewer birds use the shore as the seasons change.

title: Compare totals with another group
instruction: Put your totals next to another group's and talk about any difference.
rationale: If two groups counted the same box at the same time, their totals should be close. A big difference means someone missed birds or counted twice. Comparing is how surveyors check their counts, and it is why fair rules matter so much.

title: Check in before leaving the path
instruction: What three things keep a count fair? Why does that matter?
rationale: The survey lead checks each group's understanding before the count is filed. Each learner names the box, the time and the rules. If anyone counted a bird twice, the group sorts out how to avoid it next time. Understanding why the rules matter is what lets you run a fair survey anywhere, not just on this shore.

situation: A cyclist rings a bell coming along the shoreline path.
instruction: Move to the side of the path and let the cyclist pass.
missed: The class blocked the shared path, and the cyclist had to stop and wait until everyone moved over.

situation: The survey lead asks how you avoid counting the same bird twice.
instruction: Say you sweep the box once from left to right and count each bird once.
missed: You could not say how to avoid double counts, and the survey lead had to explain before the class went on.

explanation: You added gulls halfway through the count. Changing the rules during a count means the start and end do not match. Decide what counts before you begin, and keep it.
You chose the busiest spot to count. Picking the best spot makes the shore look busier than it is. Count in the box the survey lead marked, busy or quiet.
You counted the same bird twice when it flew back. A fair count gives each bird one tally. Sweep the box once from left to right and count only what you see on that sweep.
You started down to the waterline. The shore can be slippery, and walking close sends the birds away, which spoils the count. Count from the path with binoculars.

title: Find what you need to measure
instruction: Mark the three things that tell you the size of the bed.
rationale: To size a rectangle-shaped bed you need its length, its width and a way to see its corners. The corner stakes show where the bed begins and ends, the long side is the length, and the short side is the width. Once you have those, you can find the area and draw it on paper.

title: Put the measuring steps in order
instruction: Put the steps for finding the bed's area in order.
rationale: Finding an area has a clear order. You measure the length, measure the width, multiply them, and write the answer with its unit. Following the order means nothing gets missed and anyone can check your working. Writing each step down as you go also leaves a trail that a partner can follow to check your answer.

title: Check the tape starts at zero
instruction: Point to the zero mark at the hook end of the tape before you start.
rationale: Every measurement starts from zero. The hook end of the tape is the zero mark, so it goes on the edge you measure from. Checking it first stops a very common mistake, and crews check it every time before they cut or dig.

title: Set the scale on the drawing grid
instruction: Turn the scale dial so one grid square stands for one step of the tape.
rationale: A scale drawing uses small squares on paper to stand for real distances. Choosing the scale first means every side of the drawing matches the real bed. Garden planners draw to scale so they can plan plants before anyone digs.

title: Read the length on the tape
instruction: Commit when the marker sits where the far stake meets the tape.
rationale: Reading the tape exactly where the far stake stands gives the true length. Read straight down, not from the side, so the line you see is the right one. A careful reading here makes the area correct later. If two readers disagree, they read again together until they agree, because one wrong length makes the whole area wrong.

title: Hold the tape hook on the corner stake
instruction: Hold the hook against the corner stake while your partner reads the tape.
rationale: If the hook slips, the reading is too short. Holding it firmly against the stake keeps zero exactly on the corner. Measuring is a two-person job, one holding and one reading, just as the crew does it. The partner reading the tape calls the number out loud, and the holder repeats it, so nothing is misheard.

title: Place the bed on the drawing grid
instruction: Drag the bed outline onto the grid so its corners sit on grid points.
rationale: Putting the corners on grid points makes the scale drawing accurate. Then you can count the squares inside to check your multiplying. When the count and the sum match, you know your area is right. A drawing that matches the real bed lets the crew count how many plants fit before they buy a single one.

title: Spot the parts to add to the plan
instruction: Look at the real garden and mark each part the plan should show.
rationale: A good plan shows more than the edges. The kerb gap where water enters, the low middle where water collects and the path around the bed all matter to the crew. Adding them helps the crew plant the right things in the right places.

title: Choose the right area sum
instruction: Choose the sum that gives the area of the bed.
rationale: The area of a rectangle is its length multiplied by its width. A sum that adds them gives part of the distance round the edge instead. Choosing the multiply sum shows you know the difference between area and perimeter. Picturing the squares inside the bed is a good way to remember that area means counting space, not edges.

title: Trace the edge of the bed on the grid
instruction: Keep the marker on the edge as you trace all the way round the bed.
rationale: Tracing the edge shows the perimeter, the distance all the way round. It is different from the area, which is the space inside. Tracing both on the same drawing helps you see why they are measured differently. Crews use the perimeter to work out how much edging they need, and the area to work out how much soil.

title: Record the measurements and the area
instruction: Write the length, the width and the area with their units on the plan.
rationale: Writing every measurement with its unit lets anyone check your work. The crew uses these numbers to order soil and plants. A missing unit can cause a big mix-up, so units always go with the numbers. Numbers without units are like a recipe that says three without saying cups or spoons.

title: Check your area with another pair
instruction: Compare your area with another pair who measured the same bed.
rationale: Two pairs measuring the same bed should get about the same answer. If not, someone may have missed zero or added instead of multiplied. Checking with others is how crews catch mistakes before they order materials. Checking against another pair is quick, and it is much easier than fixing a wrong order of soil later.

title: Check in before handing the plan over
instruction: How do you find the area of the bed? Why do units matter?
rationale: The crew lead checks the plan before using it, and the class checks its understanding too. Each learner explains length times width and why units go with numbers. If anyone added instead of multiplying, the group sorts it out now.

situation: A classmate walks along the path towards the stretched tape.
instruction: Lower the tape to the ground and wait for them to pass.
missed: The tape stayed stretched, and the classmate had to stop short before stepping over it.

situation: The crew lead asks how you will work out the area.
instruction: Say you multiply the length by the width and write square units.
missed: You could not say how to find the area, and the crew lead had to explain before the class went on.

explanation: You added the length and the width. Adding them gives half the distance round the edge, not the area. Area counts the squares inside, so multiply the length by the width.
You stepped into the garden bed. Feet pack the soil hard so it cannot soak up rain. Hold the tape from the path edge, and let the stakes mark the corners.
You stretched the tape across the path where people walk. A tape at ankle height is a tripping line. Ask the crew lead to hold people back, and measure quickly, then reel it in.
You started from the tape case instead of the zero mark. The zero is at the hook end. Hold the hook on the edge of the bed and read where the other edge meets the tape.

title: Find where the water slows in the slough
instruction: Mark the three places where moving water slows down and drops its mud.
rationale: Moving water can carry tiny grains of mud. When it slows down, it cannot hold them any longer, so the grains settle to the bottom. Water slows among the marsh plants, on the inside of a channel bend and where a channel spreads onto flat ground. Those are the places where new mud builds up.

title: Read the tide board with the crew
instruction: Point to the tide board and say whether the tide is rising or falling.
rationale: Everything in a tidal marsh follows the tide. The crew reads the tide board before every job so they know how long they have before the water returns. Reading it first is a safety habit, and it also tells you whether the water is bringing mud in or carrying it out.

title: Put the tide tray test in order
instruction: Stir in the mud, run slow water, look, then run fast water with the same mud.
rationale: A fair test changes only one thing. You mix the same mud into the water each time and change only the speed. Running slow water first and fast water second, and looking closely after each, shows how speed decides where the mud settles. Looking closely after each run, before changing anything, is what keeps the two results apart.

title: Hold the plant strip in the tray
instruction: Hold the model plant strip in place until the water settles.
rationale: The plant strip stands for the marsh grass. If it lifts, the water runs under it and the test changes. Holding it steady lets you see how stems slow the water and make mud settle right among them, just as it does in a real marsh. Keeping the strip in place means the slow and fast runs both meet the same model plants.

title: Say where the mud settled
instruction: Choose the sentence that says what your two runs showed.
rationale: Your two runs used the same mud but different speeds. More mud settled when the water was slow. A good answer says that slow water drops more mud, which is why calm marshes build up. It uses your layer readings as the evidence. A careful conclusion sticks to the evidence in the table and leaves out guesses.

title: Spot how the crew helps mud build up
instruction: Look across the slough and mark each part of the crew's work.
rationale: Restoration crews help the tide bring mud where the marsh needs it. They open channels so tides can reach the marsh, lower old banks so water spreads out, and reuse dug mud to raise low spots. Each job helps the marsh gain height with the help of the water itself.

title: Set the tray's water speed
instruction: Turn the pump dial to the slow setting for the first run.
rationale: The pump dial controls how fast the water moves across the tray. Setting it exactly on slow for the first run gives you a clear starting point. Then you can turn it to fast for the second run and know that speed is the only thing that changed.

title: Read the mud layer in the tray
instruction: Commit when the marker sits at the top of the new mud layer.
rationale: The new layer shows how much mud dropped out of the water. Reading its top against the tray's scale lets you compare the slow and fast runs fairly. Slow water usually leaves the thicker layer, which is why calm marsh water builds up new ground.

title: Place a crew mat on the model mud
instruction: Drag the wide mat onto the soft mud beside the model channel.
rationale: Crews working on soft mud lay down wide mats to spread their weight, the way snowshoes work on snow. A mat keeps people and small machines from sinking and protects the mud and plants underneath. Placing it before anyone steps there is how the crew keeps the job steady.

title: Follow a cloud of mud across the tray
instruction: Keep the marker on the cloud of mud as it drifts and settles.
rationale: Following one cloud of mud shows the process as it happens. It drifts with the water, spreads out among the plants and slowly sinks to the bottom. Seeing it settle helps you explain why marshes need muddy water, not only clear water. In the real slough, each tide brings a new cloud of fine mud into the marsh.

title: Record both runs side by side
instruction: Write the layer reading for the slow run and the fast run in a table.
rationale: Two columns make the difference easy to see and easy to check. Anyone reading your table can see what changed and what stayed the same. Scientists who study the Bay's mud keep careful records like this so they can plan where marshes can grow.

title: Compare with another group
instruction: Put your table next to another group's and look for the same pattern.
rationale: If another group also finds that slow water drops more mud, the result is stronger. Comparing results is how scientists build confidence in an idea. Crews and scientists share findings about moving mud so that restoration plans work with the water.

title: Check in before the tide turns
instruction: Where does moving water drop its mud? Why does a marsh need it?
rationale: The crew finishes before the tide turns, and the class checks its ideas in time too. Each learner says where mud settles and why the marsh needs it. If anyone thinks the mud is only dirt, the group sorts it out now. Understanding moving mud helps everyone see a marsh as a living place that grows with each tide.

situation: The crew lead calls that the tide has turned and water is creeping up the channel.
instruction: Move back up the firm path with the crew and watch from higher ground.
missed: The class stayed by the channel edge, and the crew lead had to call everyone back up as the water reached the path.

situation: The crew lead asks why the crew stands on wide mats.
instruction: Say the mats spread weight so people and machines do not sink.
missed: You could not say why the crew uses mats, and the crew lead had to explain before the class could go on.

explanation: You changed the water speed and the amount of mud in the same run. With two changes you cannot tell which one made the difference. Change one thing, the speed, and keep the mud the same.
You skipped the tide board. The crew plans every job around the tide, because rising water changes where it is safe to stand. Read the board first, like the crew does.
You said the mud in the water is dirt to get rid of. Marshes are built from that mud. Each tide leaves a thin layer, and over time the layers raise the marsh so it can keep up with the water.
You started out onto the soft mud. Tidal mud can hold a boot fast, and the tide comes back in. The crew works from wide mats and boardwalks, and visitors stay on the firm path.

title: Find the kinds of plastic on the beach
instruction: Mark the three kinds of plastic you can see in the sweep strip.
rationale: Plastic reaches the shore in many forms. A bottle cap arrives whole, a bag gets torn into strips, and tiny coloured bits are what is left after sun and waves break bigger pieces apart. Seeing all three shows that plastic changes shape but does not disappear.

title: Put the float test in order
instruction: Fill the tray, drop in each piece, watch it, then sort floaters and sinkers.
rationale: The float test shows which plastics ride on the surface and which sink. Filling the tray first, dropping each piece in and watching it before sorting keeps the test tidy. Knowing which pieces float explains why some plastic washes up on beaches and some ends up in the mud.

title: Put on gloves and pick up the tongs
instruction: Put on gloves and take a pair of tongs before the sweep starts.
rationale: Gloves keep hands clean, and tongs let you pick things up without touching them. The crew uses both on every sweep, because some beach litter is sharp or dirty. Getting ready before you start means you never have to grab something with a bare hand.

title: Set the salt level in the tray
instruction: Turn the salt dial to the teacher's setting to make Bay-like water.
rationale: Salty water holds things up a little more than fresh water. Setting the salt level like Bay water makes the float test closer to what happens in the real Bay. Keeping the same salt level for every piece keeps the test fair. Scientists try to make a model as close to the real place as they can, so the results mean more.

title: Read how many pieces floated
instruction: Commit when the marker matches the size of the floater pile.
rationale: Comparing the floater and sinker piles shows how much plastic stays on the surface. Floating plastic travels with wind and tides and often washes up on beaches. Reading the pile size helps you explain why the sweep finds so much light plastic.

title: Hold the bag open for your partner
instruction: Hold the collection bag open while your partner drops the pieces in.
rationale: Holding the bag open makes the sweep quick and keeps pieces from blowing away. Working in pairs, one holding and one picking, is how the crew sweeps safely. It also means someone is always watching the waves while the other looks down.

title: Put the sharp piece in the sharps tub
instruction: Use the tongs to drag the broken glass into the sharps tub.
rationale: Sharp things never go in the soft bag, where they could cut someone later. The sharps tub has hard sides and a lid. Putting sharp pieces there straight away keeps the whole crew safe while they carry the bags. Hard sides and a lid mean nobody gets a surprise cut when the bags are lifted into the truck.

title: Spot where plastic comes from
instruction: Look along the beach and mark each way plastic reaches the shore.
rationale: Plastic reaches the beach from many places. Wind blows it from bins, storm drains carry it from streets, and waves bring it in from the water. Knowing where it comes from helps people stop it at the start, which works better than cleaning it up later.

title: Say what happens to plastic in the water
instruction: Choose the sentence that says what your test and sweep showed.
rationale: Your tray showed many plastics float, and the beach showed pieces of every size, from whole caps to tiny bits. A good answer says plastic breaks into smaller pieces but stays in the water. It does not claim more than you saw. Keeping to what you saw, and not guessing, is what makes a conclusion strong.

title: Follow a floating bag on the waves
instruction: Keep the marker on the floating bag as the waves carry it to the shore.
rationale: Following one bag shows how plastic travels. It rides on the surface, drifts with the wind and waves, and lands on the beach at the tide line. Seeing that path helps you understand why beaches collect so much floating plastic. The tide line on a beach is often where the most floating plastic gathers, which is why sweeps start there.

title: Record what you collected
instruction: Tally the caps, strips and bits your pair collected on the sweep sheet.
rationale: A tally of what was collected shows which kinds of plastic are most common. Beach crews keep these records from every sweep, so they can tell people which items to stop using. Your tally joins theirs. Totals from many sweeps show whether fewer caps and bags are reaching the shore over the months.

title: Share one way to use less plastic
instruction: Tell another group one swap that means less plastic reaches the Bay.
rationale: Stopping plastic at the start works best. Sharing swaps like a refillable bottle or a cloth bag spreads good ideas. Beach crews say the best sweep is the one that finds less than last time. A swap that a whole class makes adds up to a lot of plastic that never reaches the beach at all.

title: Check in before leaving the beach
instruction: What happens to plastic in the water? What is one way to keep it out?
rationale: The crew counts the bags and checks everyone is back before leaving. Each learner says what happens to plastic and one way to keep it out. If anyone thinks plastic melts away, the group sorts it out now. The crew also checks that every tong and glove comes back, so the kit is ready for the next sweep.

situation: A bigger wave runs up the sand towards the sweep strip.
instruction: Move up the beach with your partner, facing the water.
missed: The pair kept sweeping with their backs to the water, and the crew lead had to call them up the beach.

situation: The crew lead asks where broken glass goes.
instruction: Say sharp pieces go in the sharps tub, picked up with tongs.
missed: You could not say where sharp pieces go, and the crew lead had to explain before the sweep went on.

explanation: You reached for broken glass. Sharp things are picked up only with tongs and go into the crew's sharps tub. Call the crew lead if you see anything sharp.

You said plastic melts away in the water. Sun and waves break plastic into smaller and smaller pieces, but the pieces stay. That is why keeping plastic out of the water in the first place matters most.
You wandered off on your own. The crew sweeps in pairs inside the flagged strip so everyone stays in sight. Stay with your partner and inside the flags.
You turned your back on the waves. Waves can run up the beach further than you expect. Sweep above the wet sand line and face the water whenever you are near it.

title: Find the parts of the rain garden
instruction: Mark the three parts that help the garden soak up rain.
rationale: A rain garden is a shallow dip beside a sidewalk or roof. A gap in the kerb lets street water flow in, loose soil soaks it up like a sponge, and deep plant roots keep the soil open so water can keep moving down. Together they turn runoff into water that soaks into the ground instead of racing to a drain.

title: Put the soil test in order
instruction: Fill both columns, pour the same water on each, time it, then compare.
rationale: A fair test uses the same amount of water on each column. One column holds packed ground like a path, the other holds loose garden soil. Pouring the same water and timing each one means the soil is the only difference, so the timing tells you which one soaks water faster.

title: Wait for the crew's paint marks
instruction: Point to the paint marks and flags that show where pipes run before anyone digs.
rationale: Before any digging, a locate crew marks pipes and cables under the ground with coloured paint and small flags. The garden crew digs only once those marks are there and plans the bed around them. Waiting for the marks is a habit every digging crew keeps, because what is underground cannot be seen from above.

title: Set the cup to the same mark
instruction: Turn the dial until the measuring cup fills to the teacher's mark.
rationale: Each column must get exactly the same amount of water, or the comparison is not fair. Filling the cup to one mark and using it for both pours controls the amount. Keeping that one thing the same is what lets you trust the result you get.

title: Read the timer when the water is gone
instruction: Commit when the timer marker sits where the last water soaked in.
rationale: You stop the timer when no water is left sitting on top of the soil. Reading it at that moment for both columns makes the comparison honest. The loose soil usually wins by a long way, which is exactly the job a rain garden does in a storm.

title: Hold the column upright while it drains
instruction: Hold the soil column straight until the water stops dripping out.
rationale: If the column tips, water runs down the side instead of through the soil, and the test goes wrong. Holding it straight lets the water move through the soil the way rain moves through a garden bed. Careful handling keeps the result about the soil, not about the spill.

title: Place a plant in the garden bed
instruction: Drag the young plant to the marked spot in the bed.
rationale: Plants go where the crew's plan shows. Thirsty plants sit in the low middle where water gathers, and plants that like it drier sit on the sides. Putting each one in the right place keeps the garden healthy, so its roots keep the soil loose for years.

title: Spot how the crew works safely
instruction: Watch the crew at the garden bed and mark each safe habit.
rationale: Building a rain garden means digging near a sidewalk, so the crew keeps people and pipes safe. They leave the paint marks in place, fence off the dug bed, and wear gloves and boots when they handle soil. Each habit is part of doing the job well, not an extra.

title: Say what the soil test showed
instruction: Choose the sentence that says what your two columns showed.
rationale: Both columns got the same water. The loose garden soil soaked it up faster than the packed ground. A good answer says just that and connects it to the garden: loose soil and roots let rain soak in, so less water rushes to the storm drain.

title: Follow the water from the kerb to the soil
instruction: Keep the marker on the water as it flows through the kerb gap and spreads.
rationale: Watching the water arrive shows the garden working. It runs along the gutter, turns in at the kerb gap, spreads across the bed and slowly sinks. Seeing it disappear into the soil is the best way to understand why people call a rain garden a sponge.

title: Record both soak times
instruction: Write the soak time for packed ground and for garden soil in a table.
rationale: A table with the two times side by side makes the difference plain to anyone who reads it. It also lets another class repeat your test and compare. The crew keeps records too, noting how quickly the garden is dry after rain, to know the soil is still working.

title: Share where a rain garden could go
instruction: Show another group one place near school where rain runs off and a garden could help.
rationale: Rain gardens work best where lots of water runs off hard ground, like the edge of a car park or below a roof pipe. Sharing ideas helps the class see how many places could soak up rain. Planners look for spots the same way when they choose where gardens go.

title: Check in before the crew packs up
instruction: What does a rain garden do with the rain? Why must the soil stay loose?
rationale: The crew looks over the garden before it leaves, and the class checks its ideas the same way. Each learner says what the garden does with rain and why feet stay on the path. If anyone thinks a rain garden stays full like a pond, the group sorts it out now.

situation: A crew member pushes a full wheelbarrow of soil down the path.
instruction: Step to the side of the path and let the wheelbarrow pass.
missed: The class blocked the path, and the crew member had to set the wheelbarrow down and wait.

situation: The crew lead points at the paint on the sidewalk and asks what it is for.
instruction: Say the marks show where pipes and cables run under the ground.
missed: You could not say what the marks were for, and the crew lead had to explain before the class could go on.

explanation: You picked up a spade before the crew checked for pipes and cables. Under a sidewalk there can be water pipes and power lines. The crew has them marked with paint and flags before anyone digs, every time.

You said a rain garden stays full like a pond. A rain garden holds the water for a short while and lets it soak down into the soil. A day or so after the rain it is dry again and ready for the next storm.
You stood right on the edge of the dug bed. Fresh soil edges can crumble. Stand back on the path and let the crew work in the bed.
You walked through the rain garden. Feet press the soil hard, and hard soil cannot soak up rain. Use the path around the garden so the soil stays loose like a sponge.

title: Find the living things in the Bay
instruction: Mark the three living things you can see from the pier.
rationale: A food web starts with living things. Tiny floating plants make food from sunlight, small fish eat the tiny animals that eat those plants, and birds and seals eat the fish. Seeing each one from the pier helps you notice that they all live in the same water and depend on each other.

title: Stay behind the pier rail
instruction: Stand behind the rail on the pier deck with the naturalist.
rationale: The pier is a great place to watch the Bay, and the rail is there to keep everyone safely on the deck. Standing behind it lets you see the water without leaning out. The pier crew and the naturalist keep every group behind the rail.

title: Put one food chain in order
instruction: Put the tiny plants, tiny animals, small fish and seal in order of who eats whom.
rationale: A food chain shows one path the food energy takes. Tiny plants are eaten by tiny animals, which are eaten by small fish, which are eaten by a seal. Putting them in order shows how energy from the sun reaches a big animal in steps.

title: Hold the viewer steady over the water
instruction: Hold the pier viewer steady on the school of fish.
rationale: A steady view lets you watch the fish long enough to see them feed. Moving the viewer around makes it hard to follow them. Naturalists watch patiently in one spot, because the most interesting moments happen when you keep still. Watching for a whole minute often shows more than looking quickly at many places.

title: Say what happens if the small fish go away
instruction: Choose the sentence that says what would change if the small fish became fewer.
rationale: The small fish link the tiny animals to the birds and seals. If there were fewer of them, the birds and seals would have less to eat. A good answer follows the arrows on your web and does not guess beyond them. Thinking through what happens when one link changes is how scientists predict changes in real places.

title: Spot the web at work from the pier
instruction: Watch the water and mark each moment of feeding you see.
rationale: The food web is happening in front of you. A pelican dives for fish, a seal pops up with a fish, and small fish flash at the surface as they feed. Spotting these moments shows that the web on the board is a picture of the real Bay.

title: Turn the arrow to point the right way
instruction: Turn the arrow on the board so it points from the fish to the pelican.
rationale: Arrows in a food web point the way the food energy moves. The fish is eaten, so its energy goes to the pelican, and the arrow points to the pelican. Getting the arrows right is what turns a picture into a web that explains something.

title: Count the links for the small fish
instruction: Commit when the marker shows how many arrows touch the small fish.
rationale: The small fish has arrows coming in from what it eats and going out to what eats it. Counting them shows how important it is to the web. Animals with many links hold the web together, which is why scientists watch them closely. An animal with lots of links is a bit like a busy crossroads: many paths run through it.

title: Place the seal card on the web
instruction: Drag the seal card to its place at the top of the web.
rationale: The seal eats fish and is not eaten by anything else in this web, so it sits at the top. Placing it there shows how energy flows up to it. Every card in its right place makes the web easier to read. Animals near the top of a web depend on every link below them, so a change lower down reaches them too.

title: Follow a pelican as it hunts
instruction: Keep the marker on the pelican as it circles and dives.
rationale: Following a pelican shows a link in action. It circles, spots the fish from above and dives in. Watching it helps you remember that each arrow on the board is a real animal finding its food. Pelicans, gulls and seals all hunt the same small fish, which is why those fish sit in the middle of so many links.

title: Record the links you saw
instruction: Write each feeding link you saw from the pier with an arrow.
rationale: Writing the links with arrows turns what you saw into a small food web of your own. Anyone reading it can follow the energy from plant to fish to bird. Naturalists record sightings the same way to learn how the Bay changes through the year.

title: Compare webs with another group
instruction: Put your web next to another group's and look for the same links.
rationale: Two groups may see different links from the same pier. Comparing webs makes a bigger, fuller picture. Scientists build food webs by putting together many people's observations in exactly this way. Putting many small webs together is how scientists see the whole Bay and not just one corner of it.

title: Check in before leaving the pier
instruction: Which way do the arrows point? Why does every link matter?
rationale: The naturalist checks what each group learned before they leave the pier. Each learner says which way the arrows point and why a small animal matters. If anyone has arrows pointing the wrong way, the group sorts it out now. Getting the arrows right is the key idea, because it shows where the energy from the sun ends up.

situation: A work boat comes in to dock at the pier's landing.
instruction: Stand back from the landing so the crew can tie up.
missed: The class stayed by the landing, and the crew had to wait before they could tie the boat up.

situation: The naturalist asks which way the arrow between the fish and the seal points.
instruction: Say it points from the fish to the seal, the way the food energy goes.
missed: You could not say which way the arrow points, and the naturalist had to explain before the class could go on.

explanation: You pointed the arrow from the seal to the fish. In a food web the arrow shows where the food energy goes, so it points from the fish to the seal that eats it.
You threw a snack to the gulls. Human food is not part of the Bay food web and is not good for birds. Watch the gulls find their own food instead.
You leaned over the pier rail. Stay behind the rail and use the viewer on the deck. The pier crew keeps everyone behind the rail at all times.
You said one small animal does not matter. Tiny animals feed many fish, so a change to them reaches the birds and seals too. Every link holds the web together.

title: Find what makes the marsh a nursery
instruction: Mark the three things that help young fish and birds grow up here.
rationale: A nursery is a safe place for young animals to grow. In a tidal marsh, shallow channels keep out big fish that hunt, tall grass gives hiding places, and the mud is full of tiny animals to eat. Food, shelter and calm water together make the marsh a place where young life can start.

title: Move quietly onto the boardwalk
instruction: Walk slowly and quietly onto the boardwalk with the crew lead.
rationale: Birds nesting in the marsh notice noise and quick movement. Walking slowly and talking quietly lets you watch without making parent birds leave their nests. The restoration crew works the same way, calmly and gently, so the nursery stays a calm place.

title: Put the tide's visit in order
instruction: Put the steps of the tide coming into the marsh and going out in order.
rationale: Twice a day the tide rises and falls. As it rises, water fills the channels and brings in young fish and food. As it falls, the channels drain and the mud is left for birds to feed on. Knowing this order explains why the marsh is busy at every stage of the tide.

title: Hold the viewer still over the channel
instruction: Hold the underwater viewer still until the young fish come back.
rationale: Young fish dart away from movement and come back when all is calm. Holding the viewer still for a while lets them return so you can see them. Patience is a big part of watching wildlife, and the crew counts fish in exactly this careful way.

title: Focus the binoculars
instruction: Turn the focus wheel until the nest across the channel is sharp.
rationale: Binoculars let you see small things from far away, so you do not need to go closer. A sharp picture helps you notice details, like how the nest is hidden in the grass. Good watching from a distance is how scientists study animals without disturbing them.

title: Read the water level in the model channel
instruction: Commit when the marker sits at the water line on the channel post.
rationale: The model channel shows the tide rising and falling. Reading the water line on the post shows how deep the channel is right now. Shallow water is the key to the nursery, because it keeps the big hunters out while the small fish stay safe.

title: Place the grass clump in the model marsh
instruction: Drag the model grass clump to the bare edge of the channel.
rationale: The restoration crew plants grass along bare channel edges so young fish have more hiding places. Putting the model clump on the bare edge shows how each new plant adds shelter. A marsh with more grass along its channels can shelter more young animals.

title: Say why the marsh is a nursery
instruction: Choose the sentence that says why young animals start life here.
rationale: You saw food in the mud, hiding places in the grass and shallow water that keeps big hunters away. A good answer puts those together: the marsh is a nursery because it gives young animals food and shelter. It says what you saw and nothing more.

title: Spot the young animals in the marsh
instruction: Look from the boardwalk and mark each young animal you can see.
rationale: Spotting young animals is proof that the nursery is working. A line of ducklings behind a parent, tiny fish in a channel and a nest tucked in the grass all show that the marsh is doing its job. Crews use sightings like these to know a restored marsh is healthy.

title: Follow a young fish along the channel
instruction: Keep the marker on one young fish as it swims into the grass.
rationale: Following one fish shows how it uses the marsh. It swims along the shallow channel, then slips into the grass when something moves. Watching that shows you exactly why the grass edges matter so much to the nursery.

title: Record what you saw at each place
instruction: Write one line for the channel, the grass and the mud.
rationale: A short note for each place shows how the parts of the marsh work together. Anyone reading your notes can see where the young animals were and why. The crew keeps records the same way, so they can compare the marsh from year to year.

title: Compare sightings with another group
instruction: Put your notes next to another group's and look for the same animals.
rationale: Two groups watching the same marsh may see different things. Comparing notes gives a fuller picture of the nursery. Scientists share sightings in the same way, because many careful watchers see more than one.

title: Check in before leaving the boardwalk
instruction: Why is the marsh a nursery? What is one way people keep it calm?
rationale: The crew talks about the day before leaving, and the class does the same. Each learner says one reason the marsh is a nursery and one way visitors help. If anyone thinks the marsh is just empty mud, the group sorts it out now.

situation: A flock of birds lifts off the mud near the boardwalk.
instruction: Stop still, stay quiet and let the birds settle again.
missed: The class kept moving and talking, and the flock flew off to the far side of the marsh.

situation: The crew lead asks why they plant grass along the channel edges.
instruction: Say the grass gives young fish and birds places to hide.
missed: You could not say why the grass matters, and the crew lead had to explain before the class could go on.

explanation: You reached to scoop a young fish. Young fish are small and easily hurt. Watch them in the model channel or through the viewer, and leave the marsh's fish in the water.
You ran towards the birds. Parent birds leave their nests when people rush close, and the eggs get cold. Move slowly, stay on the boardwalk and use the binoculars to see them up close.
You stepped off the boardwalk. Marsh mud is soft and can hold a boot fast, and feet crush nests and young plants. The boardwalk is there so people can watch without harming the nursery.
You said the marsh is just mud. The mud and channels are full of small life: tiny crabs, worms and young fish. That food and shelter is why fish and birds raise their young here.

title: Find where the nutrients come from
instruction: Mark the three places nutrients can wash into the lagoon.
rationale: Nutrients are the food that plants need to grow. Rain can wash them into the water from fertiliser on lawns, from pet waste on paths and from rotting leaves. A little helps water plants, but when a lot arrives at once the algae in the water grow very fast and cloud it.

title: Put on gloves before handling samples
instruction: Put on gloves before you pick up a sample jar.
rationale: Water samples are handled with gloves as a habit, even when they look clean. Gloves keep hands clean and stop anything on your hands from getting into the sample. Water quality crews wear them every time they sample, so the class does too.

title: Put the jar test in order
instruction: Fill both jars, add plant food to one, set them in the same light, then wait and compare.
rationale: A fair test changes only one thing. Both jars get the same pond water and sit in the same light, but only one gets plant food. After a few days, any difference in the green colour belongs to the plant food, because nothing else was different.

title: Hold the sampler steady at the dock
instruction: Hold the long-handled sampler still under the water until it fills.
rationale: A steady sampler fills with water from one spot, which makes the sample fair. Stirring up the bottom mud would change the reading. Crews hold the sampler still and at the same depth every time, so samples from different days match.

title: Set the lamp to the same brightness
instruction: Turn the lamp dial until both jars get the teacher's brightness.
rationale: Algae need light to grow, so both jars must get the same light. If one jar gets more, it might go greener for that reason alone. Setting the lamp once for both jars keeps light out of the question, so only the plant food changes. In a fair test, anything you are not testing on purpose must stay exactly the same for both jars.

title: Read the colour of each jar
instruction: Commit when the marker matches the jar's colour on the green scale.
rationale: Matching each jar to a colour scale turns what you see into a reading you can compare. The greener the jar, the more algae have grown. Crews use meters that measure cloudiness to do the same job at the lagoon. Scientists always compare against a scale so that two people looking at the same jar record the same result.

title: Place the sample jar in the cool box
instruction: Drag the labelled sample jar into the cool box.
rationale: A water sample can change if it gets warm, because algae keep growing. Putting it straight into the cool box keeps it the same until it is tested. The label tells the lab where and when it was taken. Samples that sit in the sun for too long give a reading that no longer matches the lagoon they came from.

title: Say what the jars showed
instruction: Choose the sentence that says what your two jars showed.
rationale: Both jars had the same water and light. The jar with plant food turned greener. A good answer says that extra nutrients fed more algae, and it uses your colour readings as the evidence without claiming anything else. Saying only what your evidence shows is what makes a conclusion something other people can trust.

title: Spot how people keep nutrients out
instruction: Look around the lagoon and mark each thing that keeps extra nutrients out.
rationale: Keeping nutrients in balance starts on land. A strip of plants along the edge catches runoff, a pet waste bin keeps waste off the path, and a sign asks people not to feed the birds. Each one keeps a little extra food out of the water.

title: Follow runoff from the lawn to the lagoon
instruction: Keep the marker on the runoff as it flows from the lawn into the water.
rationale: Following runoff shows how nutrients travel. Rain picks up plant food from the lawn, runs across the path and reaches the lagoon. Seeing the path helps explain why what people do on land changes the water. Every garden and path that drains towards the water is part of the lagoon's story, even far from the edge.

title: Record both jars side by side
instruction: Write the colour reading for the plain jar and the plant food jar.
rationale: Two columns make the difference clear and easy to check. Anyone reading your table can see what changed and what stayed the same. Water crews keep records like this to see whether the water is getting clearer over time. A table also makes it easy to spot if you forgot a reading, because an empty box stands out straight away.

title: Share one way to keep the balance
instruction: Tell another group one thing people can do to keep extra nutrients out.
rationale: Everyone who lives near water can help keep the balance. Sharing ideas like picking up pet waste or using less lawn fertiliser spreads good habits. Crews say small changes by many people add up to clearer water. Many small habits around one lagoon can make as much difference as one big project.

title: Check in before leaving the dock
instruction: Why can too many nutrients be a problem? What is one way to keep the balance?
rationale: The crew goes over the day's samples before leaving the dock. Each learner explains what too many nutrients do and one way to help. If anyone thinks more is always better, the group sorts it out now. Talking it through together helps everyone leave with the same clear idea of balance.

situation: A splash leaves a slippery wet plank on the dock.
instruction: Step round the wet plank and tell the crew lead.
missed: The class walked straight over the wet plank, and the crew lead had to stop everyone to put a mat down.

situation: The crew lead asks which jar you are comparing the plant food jar against.
instruction: Say the plain jar is the control, with the same water and light and no plant food.
missed: You could not name the control, and the crew lead had to explain before the class could go on.

explanation: You added plant food and moved the jar into the sun at the same time. With two changes you cannot tell which one made the algae grow. Keep the light the same and change only the plant food.
You leaned over the lagoon edge. Edges can be slippery. The crew fills sample jars with a long-handled sampler from the dock, and visitors stay back from the edge.
You said more nutrients are always better. Some nutrients help plants grow, but too many feed so much algae that the water turns cloudy and green. Balance is the goal, not the most.
You went to taste the water. Water tests use kits and meters, never tasting. Wear gloves when you handle sample jars and wash hands afterwards.

title: Find the parts of the trash capture device
instruction: Mark the three parts that let water through and keep trash back.
rationale: A trash capture device sits inside a storm drain. Water comes in through the inlet, passes through a screen full of holes, and flows on to the pipe. The trash that is too big for the holes stays behind in a basket. Each part has one job, and together they let the water go and keep the trash.

title: Put on gloves before you touch the model
instruction: Put on the gloves before you pick up the model trash.
rationale: The model trash is clean, but the crew never touches drain trash without gloves, so the class practises the same habit. Gloves keep hands safe from sharp edges and dirt. Making it a habit on the easy day means it happens on the real day too. Protective equipment works only when it is worn every single time, including during practice.

title: Put the screen test in order
instruction: Pour water with no screen, look at the jar, add the screen, then pour the same again.
rationale: Pouring first with no screen shows what happens without the device. This is your control. Then you add the screen and pour the same water and trash again. The screen is the only change, so any difference in the jar belongs to the screen. Scientists call this a controlled comparison, because everything except the screen stays identical between the two pours.

title: Hold the screen in the model drain
instruction: Hold the screen flat in the model drain until its clips click.
rationale: If the screen tips, trash slips round the edge and the test is spoiled. Holding it flat until the clips click keeps it snug. Real devices are bolted in for the same reason: a gap at the edge lets trash sneak past. Engineers design the fixings carefully because water pressure during heavy rainfall pushes hard against every edge.

title: Say what the screen did
instruction: Choose the sentence that says what your two pours showed.
rationale: Both pours used the same water and trash. With the screen, less trash reached the jar, and the water still flowed. A good answer says that the screen kept trash back and let water through, with your jar readings as the proof. Scientists try to make conclusions that match their evidence exactly, without exaggerating what they observed.

title: Spot the crew's cleanout steps
instruction: Watch the crew at the real device and mark each safe step they take.
rationale: Cleaning out a device is a careful job. The crew sets cones so drivers slow down, puts a barrier round the open lid, and uses a vacuum truck so nobody has to climb in. Seeing each step shows that the cleanout is planned, not rushed.

title: Set the pour speed and leave it
instruction: Turn the tap dial to the teacher's setting and do not touch it again.
rationale: Both pours must be the same, or the test is not fair. If one pour is faster, more trash might get pushed through. Setting the tap once and leaving it keeps the flow the same, so the screen is the only thing that changes. Controlling a variable, meaning keeping it deliberately unchanged, is what makes a comparison trustworthy to other people.

title: Read the trash left in the jar
instruction: Commit when the marker sits at the top of the trash in the jar.
rationale: The jar stands for the Bay. Reading how much trash got there shows how well each pour kept trash out. Read the top of the pile at eye level, so your reading matches a classmate's. The smaller the pile, the better the screen worked. Consistent measurement habits let different observers compare their results and agree about what happened.

title: Set the basket under the screen
instruction: Drag the model basket to the spot under the screen.
rationale: The basket catches the trash the screen stops. If it sits in the wrong place, the trash piles up on the screen and blocks the water. Under the screen, it fills up neatly, so the crew can lift it out in one go. Positioning matters in engineering: the right part in the wrong place does not do its job.

title: Follow a bottle cap to the screen
instruction: Keep the marker on the bottle cap as it floats to the screen.
rationale: Following one piece of trash shows the device at work. The cap floats along with the water until it meets the screen, and there it stops while the water goes on. Watching it happen helps you explain the idea in your own words. Describing a process step by step is an important scientific skill, because it explains how a result happens.

title: Record both pours side by side
instruction: Write the jar reading for the pour without the screen and the pour with it.
rationale: Two columns side by side make the result easy to see and check. Anyone reading your table can see what changed and what stayed the same. The crew keeps a record too, noting how full each basket was, so they know how often to come back. Organised records also help the city decide where additional devices would be most useful.

title: Sort the crew's catch into groups
instruction: With gloves and tongs, help sort the model catch into bottles, bags and leaves.
rationale: Sorting shows what ends up in drains most. If most of it is wrappers, the fix starts with bins and habits on the street. The crew shares what it finds so the city knows where to put more bins and where to tell people about the drain.

title: Check in before the crew closes the lid
instruction: What does the screen let through? What does it keep back?
rationale: The crew checks the device is closed and safe before leaving, and the class checks its ideas the same way. Each learner says what the screen lets through and what it keeps. If anyone thinks the screen stops the water too, the group sorts it out now.

situation: The vacuum truck beeps and starts to back up to the drain.
instruction: Stand clear behind the barrier and wait for the truck to stop.
missed: The class stayed by the kerb, and the spotter had to stop the truck until everyone moved back.

situation: The crew lead asks why the screen is full of holes.
instruction: Say the holes let the water through so the street does not flood.
missed: You could not say why the screen has holes, and the crew lead had to explain before the class could go on.

explanation: You reached into the device. Trash can hide sharp things, and the space below the street is one only trained crew work in. The crew uses a grabber and gloves, and a truck with a vacuum lifts the rest out.
You said the screen stops the water. The holes are big enough for water and small enough to keep trash back. If it stopped the water, the street would flood, so the holes are the whole idea.
You sorted the trash with bare hands. Drain trash can be sharp or dirty. Wear the gloves the crew gives you, and use the tongs for anything that looks sharp.
You stood right by the open lid. An open drain is a place to trip. The crew puts a barrier around it, and visitors watch from behind the barrier.

title: Find where the rain goes on the street
instruction: Mark the three places the rain runs on its way to the drain.
rationale: Rain that lands on a roof, a sidewalk or a road cannot soak in, so it runs downhill. It runs off the roof into a downspout, across the sidewalk into the gutter, and along the gutter to the drain. Seeing each part shows that a whole street is one big path for water.

title: Stay on the sidewalk with the crew
instruction: Stand behind the cones on the sidewalk before the crew lead starts.
rationale: The street is for cars and the crew's truck. Standing on the sidewalk behind the cones keeps the whole class out of the way of traffic. The crew does the same every time, and only steps into the gutter once cones and a sign warn drivers to slow down.

title: Put the water's trip in order
instruction: Put the steps of the rain's trip from the roof to the Bay in order.
rationale: Water always moves downhill, so its trip has an order. It lands, runs off, joins the gutter, drops into the drain and flows through a pipe to the Bay. Putting the steps in order helps you see that the drain is not the end of the trip, only the middle.

title: Hold the watering can steady over the roof
instruction: Hold the watering can over the model roof until the rain stops.
rationale: A steady rain gives a fair test. If the can shakes or moves, some water misses the roof and the reading changes. Holding it steady over the same spot means the only thing you are watching is where the water goes once it lands.

title: Tilt the model street downhill
instruction: Turn the dial to tilt the model street towards the model Bay.
rationale: A real street is built with a gentle slope so water runs to the drain and does not pool. Tilting the model the same way lets you watch water choose the downhill path every time. The slope is the reason drains sit at the low end of the gutter.

title: Read how much water reaches the model Bay
instruction: Commit when the marker sits at the water line in the model Bay jar.
rationale: Reading the water line tells you how much of the rain ran off the street. Read it at eye level, where the water meets the side of the jar, so a classmate would read the same. It shows that almost all the rain on a hard street ends up in the Bay.

title: Place the leaf screen over the drain
instruction: Drag the model leaf screen onto the model drain.
rationale: Leaves and litter ride the water to the drain. A screen over the drain catches them before they reach the Bay. Putting it exactly on the drain shows why crews keep grates clear: a blocked grate makes the street pool, and an open one lets litter through.

title: Say where the drain water goes
instruction: Choose the sentence that says where the storm drain water goes.
rationale: Your model showed the water leaving the street and reaching the Bay. A good answer says that the storm drain carries rain to the Bay, so what we drop on the street can end up there too. It does not say more than your test and the crew's map showed.

title: Spot what does not belong in the gutter
instruction: Look along the real gutter and mark each thing that should not reach the Bay.
rationale: Anything in the gutter can ride the next rain to the Bay. A wrapper, a drip of oil under a car and a pile of leaves are all on their way. Spotting them helps you see how people on a street can keep the Bay clean before it even rains.

title: Follow the drain line on the crew's map
instruction: Keep the marker on the blue drain line from the street to the shore.
rationale: The crew's map shows pipes you cannot see under the street. Following the line from the drain to the shore shows the path the water takes underground. Crews use maps like this to find each pipe when they clean it or check it after a storm.

title: Record what you saw at each part
instruction: Write one line for the roof, the gutter, the drain and the Bay.
rationale: A short record for each part of the trip helps you remember the whole path. Anyone reading it can follow the water from the roof to the Bay. It is also how the crew keeps notes, so the next crew knows which drains need a clean.

title: Share one way to keep the drain clean
instruction: Tell another group one thing a family can do to keep the drain clean.
rationale: Many people live on one street, so keeping a drain clean is a team job. Sharing ideas, like putting litter in a bin or washing a car on the grass, spreads good habits. The crew says the drains they clean least are on the streets where neighbours help.

title: Check in before the walk ends
instruction: Where does the storm drain go? What is one thing that should never go in it?
rationale: The crew talks over each job before it packs up, so the class does the same. Each learner says where the drain water goes and names one thing that should stay out of it. If anyone thinks the drain water gets cleaned first, the group sorts it out now.

situation: A street sweeper rolls along the gutter towards the class.
instruction: Step back behind the cones and let the sweeper pass.
missed: Nobody stepped back, and the sweeper had to stop and wait for the class to clear the gutter.

situation: The crew lead asks why the water ran to the drain and not the other way.
instruction: Say that the street slopes down to the drain, and water runs downhill.
missed: You could not say why the water ran to the drain, and the crew lead had to explain the slope before the class could go on.

explanation: You said the storm drain water gets cleaned first. On many streets the storm drain runs straight to a creek or the Bay. What goes down the drain is what the fish and birds get, so only rain belongs in it.
You reached for the drain grate. Grates are heavy and the drain below is a space only trained crew enter. Look through the grate from the kerb, and let the crew open it with the right tools.
You poured soapy water into the storm drain. Soap and dirt go with it to the Bay. The crew tips wash water onto grass or into a sink, so the drain carries only rain.
You stepped off the kerb to follow the water. Cars use the street. Follow the water with your eyes from the sidewalk, and the crew sets cones before anyone works in the gutter.

title: Find the crews in the Bay projects
instruction: Mark the three crews you can see on the project photos on the wall.
rationale: Bay projects need many kinds of crews. Equipment operators dig channels and move soil, landscape crews plant rain gardens and marsh grass, and treatment plant operators run the systems that clean water. Seeing each crew at work shows that caring for the Bay is a set of real jobs people train for.

title: Greet the crew mentor
instruction: Shake hands and introduce yourself to the crew mentor.
rationale: Meeting a crew mentor is a first step into any trade. A clear greeting and your name show respect and interest. Mentors help new people learn the job, and many say the best apprentices start by asking good questions. Asking the mentor how they started in their trade is often the most useful question of the visit.

title: Put the path into a trade in order
instruction: Put the steps from learning about a trade to working on a crew in order.
rationale: Most people reach a trade through a path. They learn what the trade does, take a pre-apprenticeship to get ready, start a paid apprenticeship that mixes classes with work, and then join a crew. Knowing the order helps you plan your own path.

title: Hold up the safety gear while the mentor explains
instruction: Hold up the display hard hat while the mentor explains each piece of gear.
rationale: Safety gear is part of every trade. Holding up each piece while the mentor explains it helps you remember what it is for. Crews check their gear at the start of every shift, and learning that habit early is part of training. Each piece of gear has one job, and together they protect the head, eyes, hands and feet.

title: Say who trains workers for the clean port
instruction: Choose the sentence that matches what the Port of Oakland says.
rationale: The Port of Oakland says the Pacific Maritime Association provides skills and safety training on the zero-emission equipment, and the Machinists Institute helps the West Oakland Jobs Resource Center grow its pre-apprentice program to include careers affected by zero-emission vehicles. A good answer repeats what the source says and adds nothing.

title: Spot what the sources say about the work
instruction: Read the two source cards and mark each fact they state.
rationale: The U.S. EPA says its San Francisco Bay Program awarded more than eighty-two million dollars to twenty projects for water quality and habitat, including trash capture, green stormwater infrastructure, tidal marsh and wetland restoration, nutrient reduction, sediment management, fish habitat and PCB source control. Reading the source itself is how you know what is true.

title: Turn the job wheel to your favourite
instruction: Turn the job wheel until it points at the job you would most like to try.
rationale: Choosing a favourite job helps you notice what you enjoy, like working outdoors, running machines or caring for plants. There is no wrong choice. Careers advisers say knowing what you like is the best starting point for finding a trade that fits. Many people try more than one kind of work before they find the trade that suits them best.

title: Rate how much each job uses maths
instruction: Commit when the marker shows how much maths the chosen job uses.
rationale: Almost every trade uses maths, from measuring a rain garden to reading a gauge at a treatment plant. Rating it helps you see why school subjects matter on a crew. Mentors often say the maths they use every day is measuring, adding up and reading scales.

title: Match a job to its crew
instruction: Drag the card that says planting a rain garden to the landscape crew.
rationale: Matching jobs to crews shows how projects are shared out. Planting belongs to the landscape crew, digging to the operators and running a plant to the operators there. Knowing who does what is how crews work together safely on one site.

title: Follow one project from plan to crew
instruction: Keep the marker on the rain garden project as it moves from plan to build.
rationale: A project moves through many hands. Planners draw it, a locate crew marks pipes, operators dig, and landscape crews plant. Following one project shows how every step needs trained people, and how each crew hands on to the next. A project goes well when each crew finishes its part safely and passes on clear notes to the next.

title: Record the trades you met
instruction: Write one line for each trade you met and what it does on a Bay project.
rationale: A list of trades and their jobs is a map of possible careers. Reading it later helps you remember which work sounded interesting. Careers advisers ask students to keep lists like this when they explore pathways. Looking back at a list later often reminds people of a job they had forgotten they liked.

title: Share one job you would try
instruction: Tell another group one Bay job you would like to try and why.
rationale: Saying a goal out loud makes it real. Hearing others' choices shows how many kinds of work there are. The Port of Oakland says its clean port work will create hundreds of green jobs, with priority for people who live nearby. Hearing why a classmate likes a job can open up an idea you had not thought of yourself.

title: Check in before leaving the hall
instruction: Name two crews who work on Bay projects. How do people train for them?
rationale: The mentor checks what the class learned before they leave. Each learner names two crews and one way people train. If anyone thinks only scientists do the work, the group sorts it out now. Knowing two crews and one training path gives every learner a real starting point for their own plans.

situation: The hall's practice drill bell rings for everyone.
instruction: Line up calmly at the marked exit with the mentor.
missed: The class stayed seated, and the mentor had to gather everyone before leading them out.

situation: The mentor asks where the facts about the Bay projects come from.
instruction: Say the facts come from the U.S. EPA's award release and the Port of Oakland.
missed: You could not name the source, and the mentor had to show the class the release before going on.

explanation: You made up a number about the projects. Only say what a source says, and name the source. If a source does not say it, the honest answer is that we do not know yet.
You said only scientists restore the Bay. Scientists plan and measure, and trades crews do the building: operators, labourers, landscape crews, plant operators and many more. It takes both.

You said a new crew member can start without training. Every crew trains before the job and keeps training, from safety basics to the machines they run. Apprenticeships mix learning with paid work for exactly this reason.
You reached for the crew's harness. Safety gear is fitted and checked by trained crew. Ask the mentor to show how it is checked, and keep your hands on the display pieces.

title: Notice what you need to know
instruction: Mark the three things to notice before you do anything else.
rationale: Before acting, notice three things: whether there is any danger to you, whether the person is responding, and where exactly you are. Noticing these first keeps you safe and gives you what the person on the phone will ask for.

title: Put the call in order
instruction: Where you are, what happened, how many people, then stay on the line.
rationale: The person answering needs to know where to send help first, because that is what gets people moving. Then what happened and how many people are hurt help them send the right help; staying on the line lets them guide you until it arrives.

title: Get a trusted adult straight away
instruction: Shout for, or run to, the nearest trusted adult.
rationale: Getting an adult is almost always the fastest route to help, and it is the right first move for a young person. An adult can call, keep others back and take charge, so you are never left dealing with it alone.

title: Put the phone on speaker
instruction: Turn the phone to speaker so your hands are free and the adult can hear.
rationale: Putting the phone on speaker lets the adult beside you hear the questions and answer too, and leaves your hands free to wave to arriving help. It is a small step that makes the call work better for everyone. Every detail you can give calmly is one less question the call-taker has to ask while help is on its way.

title: Speak calmly and clearly
instruction: Commit when your voice is calm and clear enough to be understood first time.
rationale: A calm, clear voice gets information across first time; a rushed or shouted one has to be repeated, which costs time. Taking a breath before speaking is the simplest way to be understood in an emergency. Saying where you are first, before anything else, means help can start moving even if the call is cut short.

title: Stay on the line
instruction: Hold the phone and listen until they say you can hang up.
rationale: Staying on the line means the person answering can ask more questions and tell you what to do next, such as keeping the person still or waving at the arriving help. Hanging up early cuts that help off. If you are not sure what to say, the person answering will guide you with questions, so stay with them.

title: Show help where to come
instruction: Drag the waving arm to the safe spot by the road where help will arrive.
rationale: Showing arriving help exactly where to go saves time. Standing safely at the road edge, with an adult, and waving is a useful job a young person can do while trained people take over. Responders arriving at a busy place lose time finding the right spot, so a clear signal from a safe place gets them there sooner.

title: Spot the problems in a classmate's plan
instruction: Look at the classmate's help plan and mark each problem.
rationale: Help plans go wrong in predictable ways: running into danger, trying a treatment and giving a vague location. Spotting them in someone else's plan helps you remember the right order when it matters. The right order is always the same: stay safe, fetch an adult, call for help and say exactly where you are.

title: Say what you will not do
instruction: Say why you will not try to treat the injury yourself.
rationale: Knowing what not to do is part of being helpful. Leaving treatment to trained people, and doing the things you can do well, staying safe, calling and guiding, is what actually helps the person most. Trying a treatment you have not been trained in can make things worse, and it takes an adult's attention away from calling for help.

title: Stay steady until help arrives
instruction: Hold yourself in band — calm and near the adult — until help arrives.
rationale: Waiting for help is hard, and it is tempting to do something, anything. Staying calm, close to the adult and ready to answer questions is the most useful thing to do until trained people take over. Moving about or crowding round only adds to the confusion that responders then have to sort out.

title: Tell the adult what happened
instruction: When help has arrived, tell the adult what you saw.
rationale: Afterwards, telling the adult clearly what you saw helps them and the responders. Keep it to what you saw, in order, the same way a clear report is written. Guesses about what caused it can wait; the responders need what you actually saw first.

title: Share the steps with the class
instruction: Tell the class the steps: safe, adult, call, where.
rationale: Sharing the steps helps classmates remember them, and saying them out loud fixes them in your own memory. Short steps that everyone knows are exactly what helps in a real emergency. In a frightening moment people fall back on what they have practised, so the practice is the preparation.

title: Check in at the end of the lesson
instruction: How did the lesson go? Which part was hardest?
rationale: A short check-in at the end tells the teacher who is confident and who needs another go, and gives each learner a moment to notice what they can now do. Nobody is marked here, and a teacher or trusted adult is there for anyone who wants to talk more.

situation: A car pulls up fast close to where you are standing near the road.
instruction: Step back onto the pavement with the adult; do not go into the road.
missed: Nobody stepped back, and a classmate was nearly clipped by the car door. Next time, stop the lesson and deal with it first.

situation: The firefighter, playing the call handler, asks exactly where you are.
instruction: Give the street sign or landmark you noticed, clearly.
missed: You said 'near the park', and the practice responders went to the wrong side of it.

explanation: You hung up as soon as you had said what happened. The person on the phone may need to ask more questions or tell you what to do next; you stay on the line until they say you can go.

You ran straight towards the person without checking for danger. The first rule is to keep yourself safe, because a second person hurt means help has two people to reach; you look for traffic or other dangers first and get an adult.

You tried to treat the injury yourself. This lesson is about calling for help, not treating; trained people will know what to do, and trying a treatment you have not been trained in can make things worse.
You gave a vague location. Help can only arrive where you tell it to; look for a street sign, a building name or a landmark and say it clearly, because a vague answer costs time.

title: Find what the recipe card gives you
instruction: Mark the three things on the recipe card you need before scaling it.
rationale: Before scaling a recipe, find how many it serves, the list of quantities and the units each quantity is in. With those three, scaling is one calculation repeated; without them, it is guesswork. All the quantities are the ones the card itself shows.

title: Wash your hands before touching ingredients
instruction: Wash and dry your hands before the lesson starts.
rationale: Clean hands before food is the kitchen's first rule, and it applies to a maths lesson here as much as to a cooking class. Starting with it every time makes it automatic, which is exactly how professional kitchens keep food safe.

title: Put the scaling in order
instruction: Find the fraction, scale each quantity, keep the unit, then check.
rationale: Finding the scale fraction first, from how many you need compared with how many the card serves, gives you one number to use for everything. Scaling each quantity by it, keeping the units, and then checking the proportions still look right is a method that works for any recipe.

title: Level the spoon with a straight edge
instruction: Hold the spoon steady and level it off with the back of a knife.
rationale: A heaped spoon can hold a lot more than a level one, which quietly undoes careful arithmetic. Levelling each spoonful makes the measurement match the number you calculated, the same way a scientist reads a measuring cylinder at eye level.

title: Say which fraction is bigger
instruction: Say which is bigger, a half or a quarter, and why.
rationale: A half is bigger than a quarter because the whole is cut into fewer, larger parts. Being able to say why, not just which, is the understanding that stops the commonest fraction mistake.

title: Spot the problems in a classmate's scaled recipe
instruction: Look at the draft scaled recipe and mark each problem.
rationale: Scaled recipes go wrong in predictable ways: one ingredient left unscaled, a unit lost and a fraction compared the wrong way round. Spotting them in someone else's card helps you check your own.

title: Turn the recipe from whole to half
instruction: Turn the dial from the whole recipe to half, for half as many people.
