You said steel always sinks. A solid lump of steel does sink. Shaped into a hull full of air, the same steel pushes aside much more water, and the water pushes back up hard enough to hold it. It is shape, not magic.

title: Find the key, the scale and the orientation
instruction: Mark the three things on the map you read before anything else.
rationale: Every map has three things that tell you how to read it: a key that explains its symbols, a scale that links distances on paper to distances on the ground, and an orientation mark that shows which way is which. Reading those three first, on any map from any era, stops you misreading everything else.

title: Put the map reading in order
instruction: Read the label, find the key and scale, find the orientation, then read the map.
rationale: The label tells you who made the map, when and for what, which frames everything else. Key, scale and orientation then tell you how to read it, and only then do you read routes and places. The same order works on a fictional old map, a modern street plan or a satellite image.

title: Follow the archive's handling rules
instruction: Read the card: no touching originals, use the pointer and the overlay.
rationale: Old maps are fragile and some exist only once. Using the pointer and the clear overlay instead of fingers protects them from skin oils and tears, and it is how every archive keeps its collection readable for future learners.

title: Turn the old map to match the new one
instruction: Turn the old map until its orientation matches the modern map beside it.
rationale: Comparing two maps only works if they face the same way. Turning the old map to match the new one's orientation lines up the coast, roads and rivers, so real changes stand out instead of being hidden by a turned page.

title: Use the scale to estimate a distance
instruction: Commit when the dividers match the scale bar for the distance you are measuring.
rationale: Setting the dividers against the scale bar turns a gap on paper into a distance on the ground. Checking against the scale each time, rather than guessing, lets you compare the same route on maps drawn at different scales.

title: Hold the overlay still on the map
instruction: Hold the clear overlay steady over the old map while you trace the route on it.
rationale: The overlay lets you mark without touching the original, but only if it stays still. Holding it steady while you trace means your marks line up with the map, and the original stays untouched.

title: Match the old landmark to the new map
instruction: Drag the old map's harbour marker to the same place on the modern map.
rationale: Finding the same landmark on both maps anchors the comparison. Once one place is matched, you can see what moved, grew or disappeared around it, which is how historians use maps to study change over time.

title: Spot the problems in a classmate's comparison
instruction: Look at the draft map comparison and mark each problem.
rationale: Map comparisons go wrong in familiar ways: north assumed to be at the top, an old map called wrong because it differs, and no mention of who made the map. Spotting them helps you write comparisons that treat maps as the sources they are.

title: Say why the maker drew it this way
instruction: Say one reason the old map's maker might have shown some places large and left others out.
rationale: A map made for sailors shows harbours and shoals; one made for landowners shows boundaries. Asking why a maker chose what to show is reading a map as a source, and it reveals as much about the maker as about the place.

title: Follow the old road across both maps
instruction: Keep the pointer on the old road as it crosses from the old map to the new.
rationale: Following one road across two eras shows which stretches survived, which were straightened and which vanished. Tracing it carefully, without jumping to where you expect it to go, keeps your comparison based on what the maps actually show.

title: Record the comparison
instruction: Write each map's maker, purpose, orientation and the changes you found.
rationale: A written comparison that names each map's maker and purpose shows why they differ, not just that they do. It is the kind of record another historian can check against the maps themselves.

title: Return the maps to the archivist
instruction: Hand the overlays back and let the archivist return the originals.
rationale: Returning maps properly, with the archivist handling the originals, keeps the collection in order and undamaged. It finishes the lesson the way every archive visit should end, with the sources safe for the next reader.

title: Check in at the end of the visit
instruction: What surprised you about how the place changed? What was hard to read?
rationale: The archive closes its reading room by having visitors put back what they used, and the class closes by putting into words what changed between the maps and what did not. Each learner names one feature and one era; the archivist can hear who reads a map as evidence and who still reads it as a picture.

situation: A visitor sets an open drink down on the archive table beside an old map.
instruction: Politely ask for the drink to be taken outside and tell the archivist.
missed: The drink stayed on the table, was knocked over, and an old map was stained for good.

situation: The archivist asks how you know which way the old map faces.
instruction: Point to the orientation mark and say which direction is at the top.
missed: You said north is always up, and the archivist showed you the mark pointing elsewhere.

explanation: You said a map just shows what is there. Every map is made by someone for a reason, and they choose what to include, what to leave out and what to make big; reading a map as a source means asking who made it and why.

You assumed north was at the top of the old map. Many older maps put another direction at the top, depending on who made them and why; always find the map's own orientation mark before you read directions from it.

You said the old map is wrong because it differs from the new one. The place may have changed, the mapmaker may have had different tools or purposes, or both; differences are evidence to explain, not mistakes to dismiss.
You traced the route on the old map with your finger. Skin oils damage old paper and ink; in the archive you use the pointer and the clear overlay, and the archivist handles the originals.

title: Find what you need to measure
instruction: Tap the sideline, the baseline and a corner: the three lengths an arena crew needs before the floor's area and perimeter can be worked out.
rationale: Nobody tapes a whole basketball floor. The arena crew takes the sideline, the baseline and a corner to prove the rectangle is square; the key, the arc and the centre circle wait. Deciding which lengths matter is the first move in geometry, and it saves the sneakers, the tape and the afternoon.

title: Ask the caretaker for the all-clear
instruction: Catch the caretaker's eye and ask for the floor before the tape touches the hardwood.
rationale: Hardwood is a playing surface first and a geometry lesson second. The caretaker knows when the buzzer has sounded, the players have gone to the bleachers and the mop has dried the varnish. Asking for the floor is the arena's own rule, and it comes before any tape is unrolled.

title: Put the method in order
instruction: Pace it in sneakers, tape it, log it with its unit, then work the arithmetic.
rationale: Pacing the sideline in sneakers gives a rough length to hold the tape against, so a misread tape jumps out at once. Taping and logging with the unit keeps the numbers honest. The arithmetic waits until the clipboard is filled in, because a court worked from memory is a court worked twice.

title: Hold the tape taut along the line
instruction: Your classmate pins the zero at the corner. Keep the tape taut along the painted sideline until the reading settles.
rationale: A tape that sags between two corners bows like a skipping rope, and a bow is longer than the painted line beneath it. Keeping it taut and on the paint for the whole reading is the difference between the sideline's true length and a number that is always a little too big.

title: Write the length-to-width ratio
instruction: Write sideline to baseline as a ratio, then prove the same ratio holds on the drawing.
rationale: A ratio compares two lengths of the same kind, and a faithful scale drawing keeps every ratio the floor has. If sideline to baseline matches on the sheet and on the hardwood, the drawing is in proportion; if it does not, one side was scaled and the other was not.

title: Catch the mistakes in a classmate's working
instruction: Look over the worked sheet a classmate left on the bleachers and tap each slip before the coach collects it.
rationale: Reading someone else's arithmetic means following their reasoning, not only comparing answers. On a court sheet the slips are always the same three: a missing unit, a perimeter labelled as an area, and a sideline scaled while the baseline was left alone. Spotting them on a classmate's page trains the eye for your own.

title: Switch from length to area units
instruction: Both lengths are on the clipboard. Turn the unit dial from metres to square metres before the multiplication.
rationale: Area counts how many unit squares would tile the hardwood, so its unit is a square unit. Turning the dial before multiplying is a reminder that a length times a length is a new kind of quantity, and that the floor's area and its sideline can never share a unit.

title: Choose a scale that fits the page
instruction: Commit when the scale factor lets the whole floor sit on the sheet with a border, and the key is still big enough to draw.
rationale: A scale factor is a bargain. Too generous and the baseline runs off the paper; too mean and the key and the centre circle shrink to dots. Arena architects and the people who paint the lines pick round, simple factors so every helper on the crew can work the same drawing without a calculator.

title: Place the scaled length on the drawing
instruction: Drag the scaled sideline onto the sheet, then divide the baseline by the same factor and draw it too.
rationale: Every real length divided by one scale factor gives a shape the same as the hardwood but small enough for a clipboard. Once the scaled sideline and baseline are down, any angle at a corner of the drawing is the angle at the corner of the floor, which is why a coach can plan a drill on paper.

title: Keep the answer close to the estimate
instruction: Keep the calculated area in band with the paced guess while you rework the multiplication.
rationale: The paced guess is the safety net. If the calculated area is far from what the sneakers suggested, a decimal has slipped or a unit has crept in. Keeping the two in agreement while the multiplication is reworked is how an arena crew orders the right amount of varnish for the floor.

title: Record the measurements and the drawing
instruction: Log the sideline, the baseline, their unit, the scale factor and the ratio on the clipboard.
rationale: A floor nobody can re-measure from the clipboard is not finished. Logging both lengths with their unit, the scale factor and the ratio lets the coach, the caretaker or the next class reproduce the drawing and land on the same numbers. That is the line between a lucky guess and a measurement.

title: Show the class how you checked
instruction: Tell the class how the paced guess and the ratio proved the drawing true to the floor.
rationale: Saying a method aloud in front of the bleachers is the sternest test of understanding it. Showing how the paced guess caught a slipped decimal and how the ratio proved the drawing in proportion helps the classmates who stalled and fixes the idea far better than a tick on a page.

title: Check in at the end of the lesson
instruction: Before the buzzer for the next class: what went well on the floor, what was awkward, and what would you do differently?
rationale: A short huddle at the end of the session tells the coach who can tape a floor unaided and who wants another go. Nobody is graded in the huddle; the question is simply how it went and what to try next, with the coach or a trusted adult there for anyone who wants to talk more afterwards.

situation: A ball from the practice court bounces across the tape and a younger pupil sprints after it.
instruction: Stop the reading, shout a warning, and let the caretaker clear the floor before anyone steps back on the paint.
missed: Nobody shouted. The pupil caught a foot on the tape and went down, and the reading was lost anyway.

situation: The coach wanders over from the bleachers and asks what the floor's area will roughly be, before the multiplication is done.
instruction: Give the paced guess with its unit and say how the sneakers gave it to you.
missed: You had no rough figure to give, so the slip in the multiplication went unseen until it was marked.

explanation: You added the sideline and the baseline and called the total the area. Adding the sides walks the perimeter, the distance a player runs around the floor; area is the hardwood itself, sideline times baseline. Mixing them is the commonest slip on a court sheet, which is why every answer carries its unit: metres around, square metres of floor.

You added a paced length to a taped one. Paces in sneakers are a fair guess, but a stride is not a metre, and a sum that mixes them looks precise while meaning nothing. Every length on the clipboard has to be in one unit, written beside the number, or the drawing will not match the hardwood.

You walked onto the hardwood with the tape while sneakers were still squeaking. Geometry on a live court waits for the caretaker's nod: a tape across the paint is a trip line, and a player chasing a pass is watching the ball, not the floor.

You shrank the sideline to fit the sheet and left the baseline as it was. A scale drawing holds only when every length is divided by the same factor; scale one side alone and the drawing is a different rectangle from the floor, so every angle and ratio taken from it is false.

title: Find what you need before the interview
instruction: Mark the three things you need ready before the interview begins.
rationale: A good interview is prepared. A consent form sets out what will be recorded and who may hear it, a short list of open questions keeps the conversation focused without controlling it, and a working recorder means the words are kept. With those three ready, you can give your full attention to listening.

title: Put the interview in order
instruction: Consent, an easy opening, open questions with follow-ups, then thank and check.
rationale: Consent first makes the interview possible. An easy opening, such as asking where they grew up, helps the interviewee relax. Open questions and follow-ups draw out detail, and a thank-you with a check of what they are happy to share closes it respectfully.

title: Ask for consent before recording
instruction: Explain what the recording is for and ask the interviewee to agree before you press record.
rationale: Consent is the foundation of oral history. Explaining clearly what the recording is for, who will hear it and that they can stop at any time lets the interviewee make a real choice, and it is how every responsible archive works.

title: Turn the recorder's level to their voice
instruction: Turn the recording level so their voice is clear without distorting.
rationale: A recording that is too quiet loses words, and one that is too loud distorts them. Setting the level to the interviewee's voice before the main questions means their words will be heard clearly by everyone who listens later.

title: Check the voice level is in the band
instruction: Commit when the level meter sits in the band as they speak.
rationale: A level meter shows whether the voice is being recorded well. Checking it while they speak, not only in silence, catches a quiet speaker or a noisy room before the whole interview is spoiled.

title: Hold the pause while they think
instruction: Stay quiet and hold the pause while the interviewee gathers their thoughts.
rationale: The best part of an answer often comes after a pause. Staying quiet and letting the silence sit gives the interviewee time to remember, instead of jumping in with another question that cuts off what they were about to say.

title: Choose an open follow-up question
instruction: Drag the open follow-up card into the question slot.
rationale: A follow-up like tell me more about that invites detail in the interviewee's own words. Choosing it over a yes or no question keeps the story theirs, and it is the single most useful habit of a good interviewer.

title: Spot the problems in a classmate's interview plan
instruction: Look at the draft interview plan and mark each problem.
rationale: Interview plans go wrong in familiar ways: no consent step, leading questions and a plan to share recordings more widely than agreed. Spotting them helps you plan an interview that is both good history and respectful of the person.

title: Say how a memory is a source
instruction: Say what a memory can tell a historian, and what it needs checking against.
rationale: A memory tells you how something felt and what mattered to the person who lived it, which documents often miss. But memories change, so a historian checks the details against records and other accounts, weighing the memory as they would any source.

title: Keep listening through a long answer
instruction: Keep your attention on the speaker through a long answer, noting follow-ups quietly.
rationale: Long answers are where the richest stories are, and staying attentive through them shows respect as well as catching details worth asking about. Noting follow-ups quietly lets you return to them without interrupting the flow.

title: Record the archive notes
instruction: Write who was interviewed, when, what they agreed to and a summary.
rationale: An archive note tells future listeners what the recording is and what they may do with it. Writing the consent terms beside the summary protects the interviewee and makes the recording useful for years.

title: Thank the interviewee and check the sharing
instruction: Thank them and confirm what they are happy for the class archive to keep.
rationale: Closing with thanks and a check of what may be kept respects the gift of their story. It gives them the last word on how it is used, which is at the heart of every ethical oral history project.

title: Check in at the end of the session
instruction: What did the interview teach you that a book could not? What was hard?
rationale: Interviewers debrief after every recording, so the class does too: each learner says what their question drew out and what they would ask differently. Speaking about consent and listening in front of the group is practice for the real interviews, and it shows the archivist who is ready to lead one.

situation: The interviewee's voice catches while describing a hard time at work, and they look upset.
instruction: Pause the recording and gently offer to stop or take a break.
missed: You pressed on with the next question, and the interviewee ended the session upset.

situation: The oral history volunteer asks what the interviewee agreed to and who may hear the recording.
instruction: Say what the consent form covers and who may hear it.
missed: You were not sure, and the volunteer had to check the form before anything could be kept.

explanation: You asked a question that suggested its own answer. A leading question puts your idea into their memory and makes the recording less trustworthy; open questions like how, what and tell me about let them say what they actually remember.

You wrote the memory down as a proved fact. Memories are precious evidence of how things felt and what mattered, but they change over time; a historian checks them against other sources, just as they would a document.

You started recording before asking permission. An oral history belongs to the person telling it; they decide whether they are recorded, what is kept and who may hear it. Consent comes first, every time, and it can be withdrawn.

You wanted to post a clip online without asking. The interviewee agreed to a class archive, not the internet; sharing beyond what they agreed breaks their trust and their consent. Ask first, and respect the answer.

title: Sort what is on the table
instruction: Mark each item on the table that was made at the time of the events — the primary sources.
rationale: The first question a historian asks of any item is when it was made and by whom. A letter written at the time, a notice posted at the time and a photograph taken at the time are primary sources; a book written later about those events is secondary. Everything on this table belongs to the lesson's own fictional archive, labelled as such, so the method can be practised without any real claim being made.

title: Follow the archive's handling rules
instruction: Clean, dry hands, and a support under every page before you touch anything.
rationale: An archive exists so that evidence survives for every reader who comes later. Following its handling rules, clean dry hands and a support under fragile pages, is part of the historian's method, not a separate rule: damaged evidence cannot be checked again, and history depends on evidence that can be checked.

title: Question the source in order
instruction: Who made it, when, why, and for whom.
rationale: Asking who made a source, when, why and for whom tells you what kind of evidence it is before you trust what it says. A letter to a friend and a notice to the public can describe the same day very differently. Asking in this order, author first and audience last, builds a picture of the source's purpose, which is the thing most likely to shape what it leaves out.

title: Read the letter slowly, line by line
instruction: Hold your place and read the whole letter before you decide anything about it.
rationale: Reading a source all the way through before judging it stops you seizing on the first line that fits what you expected. Historians read slowly because the detail that changes the meaning is often late in a document: a date, a condition, a sentence that undercuts the rest.

title: Say where the evidence runs out
instruction: The diary has a missing page. Say what the evidence cannot tell us.
rationale: Saying where the evidence runs out is honest history, and it is often the most useful thing a historian writes. A missing page is a question for further research, not a space to fill with a likely story; naming the gap tells the next researcher exactly where to look.

title: Spot the problems in a classmate's essay
instruction: Look at the draft essay and mark each problem before it is handed in.
rationale: A history essay makes claims and backs each with evidence. The usual problems are a claim with no source, a secondary account treated as if it were a witness, and a guess written as fact. Spotting them in someone else's draft is how you learn to see them in your own, and it is exactly what a teacher will look for.

title: Turn from the primary to the secondary source
instruction: Now turn the lens from the letter to the later book that tells the same story.
rationale: Once you know what the primary source says, you can read the secondary account critically: which evidence it uses, where it agrees with the letter, and where it goes further than the letter can support. Turning deliberately from one to the other is the core skill of this lesson, and of history.

title: Judge how certain the book's claim is
instruction: Commit when your certainty matches the evidence: supported by the letter, but not proven by it alone.
rationale: Historians rarely say certainly or never; they say how strongly the evidence supports a claim. One letter agreeing with a book makes a claim more likely, not proven, because a single witness can be wrong. Judging certainty to match the evidence is what separates careful history from a confident story.

title: Link the claim to its evidence
instruction: Drag the book's main claim onto the primary source that supports it.
rationale: Tracing a claim to the evidence behind it is how historians check each other's work. Placing the book's claim beside the letter that supports it shows the reader exactly where the claim comes from, and it reveals at once any claim with nothing beneath it, which is the claim to be most careful about.

title: Keep the argument balanced as you write
instruction: Hold your conclusion in band — weighing both sources, not leaning on one.
rationale: A balanced argument gives each source its due weight: what the letter shows, what the book adds and where they differ. Leaning on one source because it says what you hoped is the easiest trap in history, and holding the balance while you write is what makes the conclusion trustworthy.

title: Record the sources, the links and the gaps
instruction: Write down each source, which claim it supports, and where the evidence runs out.
rationale: A research log lets anyone follow your reasoning back to the sources and check it for themselves. Recording the gaps as carefully as the findings tells the next researcher where the questions are, which is how historical knowledge actually grows: by one careful reader building on another.

title: Show the class how you checked the claim
instruction: Explain how you traced the book's claim to the letter and where the evidence ran out.
rationale: Showing classmates how a claim was traced to its evidence teaches the method, not just the answer, and it lets them test your reading against theirs. Historians publish their sources for exactly this reason: so that anyone can check the claim.

title: Check in at the end of the lesson
instruction: How did that go? What was difficult about questioning a source?
rationale: A short check-in lets the teacher hear what made sense and what did not, and it gives each learner a moment to name one question they still have. Nobody is graded here, and a teacher or trusted adult is there for anyone who wants to talk more.

situation: A classmate lifts a fragile page by one corner and it starts to tear.
instruction: Tell them to stop, lay the page flat on its support, and call the archivist.
missed: Nobody stopped them, and the page tore across the date line — the one detail the lesson needed.

situation: The teacher points to a sentence in your notes and asks how you know it.
instruction: Name the source the claim comes from, or say plainly that you do not yet have one.
missed: You had no source and defended the claim anyway, so it stayed in your notes as if it were fact.

explanation: You copied the secondary account's claim straight into your answer. A secondary source is someone else's interpretation, and a good historian checks its claims against the primary evidence it rests on; when you cannot find that evidence, you say so rather than repeat the claim.

You filled the gap in the diary with what probably happened and wrote it as fact. When the evidence runs out, a historian says the evidence runs out; a guess written as fact is invention, and it is how false stories about the past get started.

You picked up the fragile papers without clean, dry hands. Archive papers are damaged by grease and moisture, which is why archivists ask for clean hands and a support under the page; the archive's own rules protect the evidence for every class that comes after yours.

You accepted the letter as true because it is old. Age makes a source a primary source, not a reliable one: the writer may have been mistaken, may have wanted to persuade someone, or may have seen only part of what happened. Every source, old or new, is questioned for who made it and why.

title: Find what makes the spinner fair
instruction: Mark the three things you check before trusting a spinner.
rationale: A spinner is fair when every part is the same size, the pointer turns freely and nothing makes it stop in one place more than another. Checking those three before predicting anything means the maths describes the real spinner, not a spinner you are imagining.

title: Put the experiment in order
instruction: Check the spinner, predict, spin and tally, then compare.
rationale: Checking the spinner first and writing a prediction before spinning keeps the experiment honest, because you cannot change the prediction to match the result. Spinning and tallying many times, and only then comparing, is how any probability experiment is run, from a classroom to a lab.

title: Agree what the prizes are
instruction: Read the stall card: stickers only, nothing to pay, nothing to lose.
rationale: This lesson is about how chance works, so the stall uses stickers and nobody pays or loses anything. Being clear about that from the start matters, because the same maths explains why games where money is at stake are built so that, over time, the players lose.

title: Give the pointer a full spin
instruction: Turn the pointer firmly so it goes round more than once before it stops.
rationale: A gentle nudge that barely moves the pointer lets the starting position decide the result. Spinning firmly, so the pointer goes round several times, is what makes each outcome depend on chance alone and not on where you started.

title: Read which part the pointer stopped on
instruction: Commit when you can see clearly which part the pointer's tip is in.
rationale: A result only counts once you can see which part the pointer's tip sits in. If it lands on a line, the stall's rule is to spin again, decided before the game starts, so that nobody chooses the result they would prefer.

title: Hold the board level while it spins
instruction: Hold the spinner board steady and level while the pointer turns.
rationale: If the board tilts, the pointer tends to settle at the lowest point, and the spinner stops being fair even if its parts are equal. Holding it level while it turns is part of running a fair test, the same as keeping any other condition the same between trials.

title: Add the result to the tally
instruction: Drag the tally mark to the row for the part the pointer stopped on.
rationale: A tally is a running record, one mark per spin in the row it belongs to. Putting each mark in the right row as it happens, rather than trying to remember a string of results, is what makes the final count something you can trust.

title: Spot the problems in a classmate's report
instruction: Look at the draft experiment report and mark each problem.
rationale: Probability reports go wrong in a few familiar ways: a prediction written after the spins, a conclusion drawn from too few trials and an outcome called due. Spotting them in another report is how you learn to write a conclusion that the evidence actually supports.

title: Say the chance of landing on one part
instruction: The spinner has equal parts. Say the chance of one of them as a fraction.
rationale: With equal parts, the chance of one part is one out of the number of parts, written as a fraction. Saying it as a fraction, and why, links probability to the fractions you already know and gives a prediction you can test.

title: Keep the tally going through a long run
instruction: Keep up with the spins, marking each one as it lands.
rationale: The point of many spins is that short-run wobbles even out, but only if every spin is counted. Keeping up through a long run, without skipping or double-counting, is where concentration matters more than arithmetic.

title: Record the prediction and the results
instruction: Write the prediction, the tally totals and how they compare.
rationale: Writing the prediction beside the results shows how close chance came to what equal parts predicted. The record is what lets someone else repeat your experiment and see whether they get a similar pattern.

title: Pool your results with the class
instruction: Add your tally to the class total on the board.
rationale: Pooling everyone's spins gives a much longer run than any one group could manage, and the class total usually sits closer to the prediction than any single group's. Seeing that happen is the clearest evidence that more trials give a better picture.

title: Check in at the end of the lesson
instruction: What surprised you about the spins? What would you test next?
rationale: The stall closes with the class comparing what they expected the spinner to do with what it did. That gap between the guess and the tally is the whole lesson in chance, and hearing classmates describe it in their own words helps the ones who still think a spinner remembers its last spin.

situation: A small child who is not in your class is standing alone and crying at the tent entrance.
instruction: Tell the stall volunteer straight away; stay where you are with your group.
missed: Nobody told an adult, and the child wandered off into the crowd before anyone could help.

situation: The stall volunteer asks your group whether their spinner is fair and how you would know.
instruction: Say what you checked about the spinner and what the long run shows.
missed: You said it was fair because you won, and the volunteer pointed out that proves nothing.

explanation: You counted how many colours there are and ignored how big each part is. Chance depends on the share of the spinner each outcome takes up, so a spinner with one big part and two small ones is not an equal three-way chance.

You said red is due because it has not come up for a while. A fair spinner has no memory: each spin has the same chance as the last, whatever came before. Believing an outcome is due is the gambler's mistake, and it is why games of chance are not a way to win anything back.

You decided the spinner was unfair after a handful of spins. Short runs wobble a lot by chance alone; only many spins show whether the results settle near what equal parts predict, and even then you check the spinner itself.

You stepped back across the tent's guy ropes to get a better view. Guy ropes are a trip hazard at every fair; you watch from inside the tent, and the volunteer keeps the ropes flagged so nobody walks into them.

title: Find what a good talk needs
instruction: Mark the three things you need before you step up to speak.
rationale: A talk that works has one clear message you want the audience to remember, a shape with a beginning, middle and end, and prompt cards with key words rather than a full script. With those three ready, you can concentrate on speaking to people instead of reading at them.

title: Learn the stage safety marks
instruction: Read the stage manager's card: stay inside the taped area, keep clear of the edge.
rationale: A stage has a real drop at its edge, cables, and lights that can dazzle. Knowing where the taped speaking area is before you start means you can move naturally without thinking about where your feet are, which is exactly why actors walk the stage before a show.

title: Put the talk plan in order
instruction: Choose the message, plan the opening, build the middle, then plan the ending.
rationale: Choosing your message first makes every other choice easier: the opening introduces it, the middle supports it and the ending repeats it. Planning in that order gives a talk a clear line from start to finish, which is what audiences follow and remember.

title: Hold a slow breath before you begin
instruction: Stand still and hold a slow, steady breath before your first line.
rationale: A slow breath before speaking calms your heartbeat and steadies your voice. Standing still for that moment also signals to the audience that you are about to begin, and it gives you time to find your first line instead of rushing into it.

title: Say why one message beats many
instruction: Say why a talk with one clear message is remembered better than one with many.
rationale: Listeners cannot flip back a page, so they remember what is clear and repeated. One message, supported and repeated, gives them something to take home; many messages compete and are lost. Saying why is understanding how talks work.

title: Spot the problems in a classmate's talk plan
instruction: Look at the draft talk plan and mark each problem.
rationale: Talk plans go wrong in familiar ways: no clear message, a full script to read and an ending that stops without repeating the point. Spotting them in someone else's plan helps you build a stronger one of your own.

title: Turn to face the whole audience
instruction: Turn so you face the middle of the audience, not the teacher or the wall.
rationale: Facing the middle of the audience lets your voice carry to everyone and lets them see your face. Turning to one person or the screen shuts out the rest of the room, and it is one of the simplest habits that makes a speaker easy to follow.

title: Pitch your voice to the back row
instruction: Commit when the voice meter shows you would be heard at the back.
rationale: Speaking to the back row, not the front, makes sure everyone hears without you shouting. It is about projecting from your chest and speaking clearly, and stage managers check it with a friend at the back before every show.

title: Put the prompt card in your hand
instruction: Drag the key-word prompt card to your hand, leaving the full script on the table.
rationale: A prompt card with a few key words keeps your place while letting you look up. Leaving the full script behind stops the temptation to read, and it is what experienced speakers do so that they talk to people rather than to paper.

title: Keep your pace steady through the talk
instruction: Keep your speaking pace in the band, not rushing as nerves build.
rationale: Nerves speed speakers up, and a rushed talk is hard to follow. Keeping a steady pace, with small pauses between points, gives the audience time to take in each idea, and it makes you sound calmer than you might feel.

title: Record feedback on your talk
instruction: Write one thing that went well and one thing to try next time.
rationale: Writing one strength and one next step turns a talk into practice for the next one. It keeps the focus on getting better rather than on being perfect, and it gives you something clear to work on.

title: Thank the audience and invite questions
instruction: Thank the audience and invite questions, listening fully before you answer.
rationale: Thanking the audience and inviting questions ends a talk warmly and shows respect. Listening to the whole question before answering, and saying if you do not know, is what makes questions a conversation rather than a test.

title: Check in at the end of the rehearsal
instruction: How did it feel to speak? What would help you next time?
rationale: Every performer gets notes after a run, so each learner leaves the stage with one thing that landed and one thing to work on next time, said kindly and specifically. Hearing the notes given well is itself the lesson in feedback, and the theatre's stage manager can see who is ready to speak again.

situation: A stage light flickers and goes out, leaving part of the stage dim.
instruction: Stand still where you are and wait for the stage manager's instruction.
missed: You walked towards the wings in the dark and caught a cable, nearly falling off the stage.

situation: The stage manager asks what the one thing is that you want the audience to remember.
instruction: Say your one clear message in a single sentence.
missed: You listed several ideas, and the stage manager asked you to choose one before you went on.

explanation: You tried to squeeze in every point you could think of. Listeners remember a few things, not many; a talk with one clear message and a few supporting points is remembered, while a crowded one is forgotten by the time you sit down.

You decided your nerves meant you could not do it. Nearly every speaker feels nervous; slow breathing, a planned first line and a friendly face in the audience help, and the nerves usually ease once you start.

You read every word from the page with your head down. The audience loses your face and your voice goes flat; short prompt cards with key words let you look up, speak naturally and still keep your place.
You stepped backwards towards the edge of the stage. Stage edges are marked for a reason and the drop is real; speakers stay on the marked area, and the stage manager keeps the edge lit and taped.

title: Find what the map gives you
instruction: Mark the three things on the map board you need to work out the journey.
rationale: Before measuring anything, find what the map provides: the scale bar that links map length to real distance, the start and the destination, and the route between them. With these three a map becomes a calculation, and without any one of them it is only a picture.

title: Put the method in order
instruction: Measure on the map, scale it up, choose the speed, then work out the time.
rationale: The order follows the reasoning: you cannot scale a length you have not measured, and you cannot find a time until you know the real distance and the speed. Working in this order, and writing each result with its unit, means anyone can follow the working and find a slip.

title: Read the map from behind the rope
instruction: Stand behind the landing rope where the board is meant to be read.
rationale: At a ferry landing, the rope marks where people wait safely while the boat comes in. The map board is placed to be read from that side; staying behind the rope is the landing's own rule, and following a site's rules comes before any lesson held there.

title: Convert the time into matching units
instruction: The speed is per hour. Turn the dial so the time is worked in hours too.
rationale: Speed, distance and time only fit together when the units match. Converting before calculating, rather than after, avoids the commonest error in this topic, and writing the unit at each step shows you checked.

title: Choose a sensible walking speed
instruction: Commit when the speed is a sensible walking pace for a class — not a run, not a crawl.
rationale: A calculation is only as good as the numbers put into it. Choosing a sensible speed for the way the class will actually travel makes the time realistic, and questioning whether an input makes sense is a skill every good problem-solver uses.

title: Trace the route with the string
instruction: Hold the string along the winding route from start to end.
rationale: A winding route cannot be measured with a straight ruler, so the string follows every bend and is then straightened against the ruler. Holding it carefully along the route gives the true path length, the same trick map readers have always used.

title: Put the journey time on the timetable
instruction: Drag the journey time onto the class timetable to see when you arrive.
rationale: Placing the journey time on the day's timetable turns a calculation into a plan: it shows when the class arrives and whether it fits before the ferry leaves. This is why people work out journey times at all.

title: Spot the problems in a classmate's route plan
instruction: Look at the draft route plan and mark each problem.
rationale: Route plans go wrong in predictable ways: a straight line measured where the path winds, a map length used without the scale, and units mixed in the time. Spotting them in someone else's plan teaches you to check your own before the class sets off.

title: Check the answer against common sense
instruction: Ask whether the journey time is believable for that walk.
rationale: A quick sense check catches the big errors: a walk across a small park should not take a day, and a long route should not take moments. If the answer looks wrong it probably is, and the usual culprit is a missed scale or mixed units.

title: Keep the class on pace along the route
instruction: Hold the pace in band as the class walks the route.
rationale: A journey time assumes a steady pace. Keeping the class near that pace, not racing ahead or falling behind, is how the plan holds, and noticing when it slips is how you know to adjust the arrival time.

title: Record the route and the working
instruction: Write down the map length, the scale, the real distance, the speed and the time.
rationale: Recording each step with its unit means the plan can be checked and reused. It also shows exactly where a mistake happened if the class arrives at a different time than expected.

title: Show the class your sense check
instruction: Explain how you checked the time made sense.
rationale: Explaining a sense check out loud helps classmates who trusted a strange answer, and it fixes the habit in your own mind. Checking whether an answer is believable is one of the most useful things mathematics teaches.

title: Check in at the end of the lesson
instruction: How did the route go? What was hard, and what would you try next time?
rationale: A short check-in at the end tells the teacher who is confident and who needs another go, and it gives every learner a moment to notice what they learned. Nobody is graded here, and the teacher or a trusted adult is there for anyone who found the lesson hard and wants to talk it through.

situation: The ferry horn sounds and a classmate walks towards the edge to watch it dock.
instruction: Call them back behind the rope and keep the group together until the attendant says it is clear.
missed: Nobody called them back, and the attendant had to stop the docking while they were moved.

situation: The teacher asks how far the route really is, not how long it is on the map.
instruction: Give the real distance with its unit and say how the scale gave it.
missed: You gave the map length, and the time worked from it was far too short. Next time, stop the lesson and deal with it first.

explanation: You used the ruler reading on the map as if it were the real distance. A map is a scale drawing, so every length on it has to be multiplied by the scale to give the real distance; without that step the journey is impossibly short.

You measured straight across the water for a route that has to go round by the path. A journey's distance is the length of the route actually travelled, not the straight line between the ends; measuring the wrong one makes the time wrong too.

You mixed minutes and hours in one calculation. Speed, distance and time only fit together when the units match, so a speed per hour needs a time in hours; mixing them gives an answer that is wildly out.

You stepped past the rope at the ferry landing to read the map. The rope keeps people back from the edge while the ferry comes in, and the map board is placed so it can be read from the safe side; the lesson waits on the right side of the rope.

title: Find the parts of the label
instruction: Mark the three parts of the safety label you must read before using the product.
rationale: A safety label is organised so the most important information is easy to find: a signal word that says how serious the warning is, a picture that shows the kind of danger, and the instructions for what to do and what to do if something goes wrong. Knowing where each part is means you can read any label quickly and completely, whatever the product.

title: Read the instructions all the way through
instruction: Before you touch anything, read every step to the end.
rationale: Reading instructions all the way through before starting shows you what you will need, how long it will take and where the warnings are. It is the habit that separates people who finish a task smoothly from people who stop halfway to find something they needed at the start, and it applies to a recipe, a game or a form.

title: Put the reading routine in order
instruction: Title, what you need, the steps, then the warnings and what to do if it goes wrong.
rationale: Reading in a fixed routine makes any set of instructions manageable: the title says what it is for, the list of what you need lets you gather it first, the steps say what to do and the warnings say what to avoid. Following the same routine every time means nothing important gets missed, however long or unfamiliar the instructions are.

title: Keep your place as you read the steps
instruction: Trace each line as you read so you do not skip a step.
rationale: Keeping your place, with a finger or a ruler under the line, stops the eye jumping ahead and missing a step that looks like the one before it. Careful readers of instructions do this with anything that matters, because a skipped step is often the one that makes the rest work.

title: Ask the teacher about the part you are unsure of
instruction: One instruction could be read two ways. Ask the teacher which it means.
rationale: When an instruction can be read two ways, asking is the skilled thing to do, not a sign of weakness. Adults at work ask the same question every day, and the person who wrote the instruction would always rather be asked than have it done wrongly.

title: Spot the problems in badly written instructions
instruction: Look at the classmate's draft instructions and mark each problem.
rationale: Writing instructions is the best way to learn to read them. Badly written instructions usually give steps out of order, use a word the reader will not know without explaining it, and leave out what to do if something goes wrong. Spotting these in a draft teaches you to notice them in real instructions, and to ask about them.

title: Look up the word you do not know
instruction: One word in step four is new. Turn the dial from the word to its meaning before going on.
rationale: An unfamiliar word in an instruction is a signal to stop, not to guess. Looking it up, in a glossary, a dictionary or by asking, means you follow the instruction that was written rather than the one you imagined; in safety instructions especially, one misunderstood word can change what you do.

title: Read at a pace that lets you understand
instruction: Commit when your reading pace is steady — not rushing, not stopping on every word.
rationale: Reading too fast skims over the details that matter; reading too slowly loses the thread of what the steps are building towards. A steady pace, slowing down only for warnings and new words, is how skilled readers take in instructions accurately.

title: Return the product to its labelled place
instruction: Drag the bottle back to its labelled shelf, still in its own container, when you are done.
rationale: A product kept in its own labelled container, in its labelled place, can always be read by the next person who uses it. Putting it back properly finishes the task and protects everyone who comes after you, which is the reason labels exist in the first place.

title: Keep your focus while you follow the steps
instruction: Hold your attention in band as you carry out each step, checking back to the page.
rationale: Following instructions well means looking back at the page between steps rather than working from memory after the first read. Keeping your focus on the page and the task together is what stops small slips turning into a finished job that does not work.

title: Record what you read and what you asked
instruction: Write down the label parts, the new word and the question you asked.
rationale: Recording what you read, the word you looked up and the question you asked shows your teacher how you worked, not just whether you finished. It also gives you a record to look back on the next time you meet a label or a set of instructions like it.

title: Share one reading tip with the class
instruction: Tell the class one thing that helped you read the instructions well.
rationale: Sharing a reading tip with classmates helps the ones who found it hard and fixes the habit in your own memory. The best tips are simple, read it all first, keep your place, ask when unsure, and everyone in the class can use them tomorrow.

title: Check in at the end of the lesson
instruction: How did that go? Which part of reading the label was hardest?
rationale: A short check-in at the end tells the teacher who is confident and who needs another go, and it gives each learner a moment to notice what they can now do. Nobody is marked here, and a teacher or trusted adult is there for anyone who wants to talk more.

situation: A classmate knocks over an open bottle and it starts to spill across the bench.
instruction: Step back, keep others back, and tell the teacher — the label says what to do next.
missed: Nobody told the teacher, and a classmate wiped it up with bare hands before anyone read the label.

situation: The workshop technician points at the label and asks what its signal word tells you.
instruction: Say what the signal word shows about how serious the warning is, in your own words.
missed: You could not say what it meant, so the technician kept the product off your bench.

explanation: You guessed what the picture on the label meant. Safety pictures are chosen to be understood quickly, but a guess can be wrong, and the words beside the picture say exactly what it means; when you are unsure, you read the words or ask, you do not guess.

You poured some of the product into an empty drinks bottle. A product separated from its label has lost its warnings and its first-aid instructions, and a drinks bottle invites someone to drink from it; products stay in their own labelled containers.

You skipped the section on what to do if something goes wrong. That section is written for the moment when there is no time to read, which is exactly why it has to be read beforehand; knowing it already is what lets you act calmly and get an adult quickly.

You started on step one before reading to the end. Instructions often put an important warning or a thing you need later near the bottom, and discovering it halfway through a task is how people get stuck or hurt. Reading the whole set first is the single most useful reading habit for life.

title: Find the robot's sensors
instruction: Mark the floor scanner, the light curtain and the camera around the robot cell.
rationale: A robot cannot see or hear like you. It uses sensors: a floor scanner that measures how far away things are, a light curtain that notices when a beam is broken, and sometimes a camera. Each one sends a signal to the robot's controller, which decides whether to keep going, slow down or stop.

title: Stand on the visitor line
instruction: Join the technician on the painted visitor line outside the fence.
rationale: Robot labs have painted lines that show where visitors stand. The line is outside every zone, so the robot can keep working while you watch. The technician explains from the line too, because everyone, even the experts, follows the same rules near a working robot.

title: Put the robot's reactions in order
instruction: Order what the robot does as a person walks closer and closer.
rationale: The robot reacts in steps. Far away, it works at its normal speed. When someone enters the warning zone, it slows down. If they come into the stop zone, it stops and holds still. Only after the person leaves and the technician checks does it start again. Each step depends on how close the person is.

title: Hold still in the warning zone
instruction: Stand still on the yellow warning zone and hold while the robot slows down.
rationale: Standing still in the warning zone lets you watch the robot change speed because of you. The scanner measured your distance, the controller compared it with the zone, and the arm slowed. Holding still long enough shows that the robot keeps slowing for as long as someone is close.

title: Turn the dial to set the warning zone
instruction: Turn the model dial slowly to make the warning zone bigger around the robot.
rationale: A bigger warning zone gives the robot more room to slow down before anyone gets close. Turning the dial on the model shows the yellow ring growing. Real zones are set by trained people using the robot's speed and how quickly it can stop, and they are tested before anyone relies on them.

title: Read the distance on the scanner screen
instruction: Commit when the marker shows the person standing outside the stop zone.
rationale: The scanner screen shows how far away the nearest person is. When the marker sits outside the red stop zone, the robot is allowed to keep moving slowly. Reading the screen shows that the robot's choice comes from a measurement, not from guessing, which is why a working sensor matters.

title: Move the cone back to the line
instruction: Drag the traffic cone back onto the painted visitor line.
rationale: Cones and lines only work if they stay where they belong. A cone pushed inside the zone could make people think the safe area is bigger than it is. Putting it back on the line keeps the message clear for the next visitor, just as technicians do at the start of every shift.

title: Say who may start the robot again
instruction: Choose the sentence that says who restarts the robot and what they check first.
rationale: When a robot stops for a person, starting it again is a decision, not a button anyone can press. A good answer says the trained person in charge restarts it, and only after checking that nobody is inside the zones. It uses what you saw when the technician walked round the fence.

title: Spot the people who work with robots
instruction: Look round the lab and mark three kinds of work people do with robots.
rationale: Many people work with robots. Operators run them and keep the area clear. Technicians mend them and check the sensors. Robot trainers show robots how to do a task and test whether they learned it well. These are jobs people train for, and each one uses the ideas in this lesson.

title: Follow the robot arm as it moves
instruction: Keep the marker on the robot's gripper as it picks up a block and puts it down.
rationale: Following the gripper shows how the arm moves in arcs, not straight lines, which is why the zones are round. The arm can swing farther than it looks. Watching it from the line helps you see why nobody stands near a robot that is working, even when it seems far away.

title: Record what made the robot slow and stop
instruction: Write what the robot did when you were far, in the warning zone and in the stop zone.
rationale: Three short lines tell the story: far away it worked, in the warning zone it slowed, in the stop zone it stopped. A record like this lets you check your thinking later. Technicians keep records of every sensor test for the same reason, so the next person knows it was checked.

title: Swap a question with a partner
instruction: Ask a partner one question about how robots sense people, then answer one of theirs.
rationale: Asking and answering questions shows what you understand and what you still wonder about. A good question might be what happens if a sensor breaks. Robot teams ask each other questions all the time, because asking early is how problems get found before anyone is near the arm.

title: Check in at the visitor line
instruction: How does the robot know you are near? Who may start it again?
rationale: The technician ends the visit by checking what everyone learned. Each learner names one sensor and says who restarts the robot. If anyone still thinks the robot sees like a person, the group works it out together before leaving the lab.

situation: The robot has stopped because a visitor stepped too close to the gate.
instruction: Stay on the visitor line and wait while the technician checks the zones.
missed: The class drifted toward the gate after the stop. When a robot stops, stay on the line and wait for the technician.

situation: The technician asks how the robot knew to slow down.
instruction: Say the floor scanner measured how far away the person was and the robot slowed for the zone.
missed: You could not say how the robot knew, and the technician explained before the class went on.

explanation: You tried to sneak past the scanner. The scanner is how the robot knows someone is near. Tricking it does not make the robot safe, it only makes it blind. Walk where everyone can be seen, and let the scanner do its job.
You went to press start. Only the trained person in charge starts a robot again, after checking that everyone is out of the zones. A visitor never presses start, even when the robot looks ready.

You reached toward the fence to touch the arm. A robot arm can move quickly and does not feel you the way a person would. The fence and the zones are there so hands stay outside; the technician shows the arm up close only when it is switched off and locked.

You said the robot sees like a person. It does not. Its sensors measure things like distance or light and send numbers to its controller. It only knows what its sensors tell it, which is why the zones and the stop button matter so much.

title: Find who is in the loop
instruction: Mark the job screen, the rule-checker box and the OK desk around the practice robot.
rationale: A robot job does not go straight from a program to a robot. It passes through a loop of people and checks. The job screen is where the helper program writes its ask. The rule-checker box looks at the ask and lights a lamp. The OK desk is where the grown-up in charge sits and decides. Finding all three shows you the whole path.

title: Stand at the OK desk
instruction: Join the supervisor at the OK desk, outside the keep-away ring.
rationale: The OK desk sits outside the ring on purpose. From there the supervisor can see the robot, the ring, the stop button and the screen all at once. Standing beside the supervisor lets you watch a real decision being made, and it keeps you where the robot's space stays clear.

title: Put a robot job's journey in order
instruction: Order what happens from the program's ask to the robot's work.
rationale: A job travels in steps. First the program asks for it. Next the rule checker looks at it and lights green or red. Then the grown-up in charge reads it and says OK or no. Only then does the robot start, and someone watches it the whole way with a hand near the stop. Each step waits for the one before it.

title: Keep a hand near the stop
instruction: Hold the watcher's pad while the practice robot does its job.
rationale: Saying OK is not the end of the grown-up's work. Someone watches the robot for the whole job, with a hand near the stop button. Holding the watcher's pad shows what that feels like: steady, patient and ready. If anything looks wrong, the watcher presses stop and the robot holds still at once.

title: Pick the job that gets a no
instruction: Choose the job card the rule checker and the grown-up would turn down.
rationale: Not every ask gets an OK. A job that wants the robot to go fast while a person stands close gets a no. So does a job that is not on the list of things this robot is allowed to do. Picking the card that gets a no shows you understand that the answer depends on the rules, not on how nicely the program asks.

title: Find the reasons the checker says no
instruction: Mark the three lamps on the rule-checker box that mean no.
rationale: The rule checker has a lamp for each reason it can say no. One lamp means the stop button is pressed, and nothing moves until a person resets it. One means somebody is standing too close to the robot. One means the job is not on the list this robot is allowed to do. When any of these lamps is lit, the job waits.

title: Turn the dial to set the keep-away ring
instruction: Turn the model dial slowly to make the keep-away ring wider around the practice robot.
rationale: The keep-away ring is the space the robot needs to itself while it works. The rule checker uses the ring to decide whether somebody is too close. Turning the dial shows the ring growing on the floor. In a real lab, trained people set the ring from how fast the robot moves and how quickly it can stop, and they test it before anyone relies on it.

title: Read the speed on the job card
instruction: Commit when the marker on the speed meter sits inside the slow band the job is allowed.
rationale: Every job card says how fast the robot may move. The rule checker compares that speed with the limit for this robot and this lab. Reading the meter shows that the OK comes from a measurement that anyone can check, not from a guess. A job that asks for more speed than the band allows gets a no.

title: Put the job card in the OK tray
instruction: Drag the checked job card from the screen onto the tray on the OK desk.
rationale: A job that has passed the rule checker is still only an ask until the grown-up in charge has read it. Moving the card to the OK tray is how the lab shows whose turn it is to decide. The card waits in the tray while the supervisor looks at the ring, the lamps and the stop, and then says OK or no.

title: Follow the robot as it works
instruction: Keep the marker on the practice robot's gripper from the first move to the last.
rationale: Watching the robot for the whole job is part of the OK. The supervisor follows the gripper and compares what the robot does with what the job card said it would do. If the robot does something the card did not say, the watcher presses stop. Following the gripper from start to finish shows how much attention a watcher gives.

title: Write down the decision and the reason
instruction: Write what the grown-up decided about the job and the reason behind it.
rationale: Every decision at the OK desk goes in the logbook: what the program asked, what the rule checker showed, what the grown-up said and why. A logbook like this lets anyone check later that the rules were followed. Robot labs keep records of every job for the same reason, so the next person knows what happened.

title: Swap a question with a partner
instruction: Ask a partner one question about who may say OK to a robot, then answer one of theirs.
rationale: Asking and answering questions shows what you understand and what you still wonder about. A good question might be what happens if the program asks again after a no. Robot teams ask each other questions like this before every new job, because asking early is how problems get found while they are still small.

title: Check in at the OK desk
instruction: Who says OK before a robot starts a job a program asked for? What always wins?
rationale: The supervisor ends the visit by checking what everyone learned. Each learner says who gives the OK and what wins over everything else. If anyone still thinks the program is in charge of the robot, the group talks it through together before leaving the lab.

situation: The helper program has sent the same job again and asks for the robot to go faster.
instruction: Say no: the faster job is over the speed band, so it waits.
missed: The faster job sat on the screen with nobody saying no, and the supervisor turned it down before the class went on.

situation: A classmate has stepped inside the keep-away ring while the practice robot is working.
instruction: Press the stop and wait on the OK side of the ring while the supervisor clears the space.
missed: The robot kept working with someone inside the ring until the supervisor pressed stop. The watcher presses stop first.

explanation: You covered the stop button. The stop button must be easy to reach and easy to see for the whole job. Covering it makes the robot harder to stop, not safer. The supervisor keeps it clear and keeps a hand near it while the robot works.

You went to press OK. A polite ask is still only an ask. The OK belongs to the grown-up in charge, who has looked at the job, the ring and the stop lamp first. A visitor never gives a robot its OK, however friendly the message on the screen looks.

You said the program is in charge. It is not. A program can ask for a job, and that is all. The rule checker can say no, the grown-up can say no, and the stop button wins over everything. People stay in charge of what a robot does, every single time.

You let the job start with someone inside the ring. The rule checker would say no to that, and so would the grown-up. The ring is the robot's keep-away space. Nobody is inside it when a job starts, and the job waits until the space is clear.

title: Find the tools that catch the dust
instruction: Mark the three things the crew uses to keep drilling dust out of the air.
rationale: A crew drilling concrete has more than one way to catch dust. A shroud around the drill bit pulls dust into a vacuum hose, a water line keeps a bigger drill wet so the dust turns to mud, and a special vacuum cleans the holes afterwards. Each one stops dust before it reaches the air people breathe.

title: Put the dust test in order
instruction: Lay a clean dark card, drill the model without the shroud, look at the card, then a fresh card and drill with the shroud on.
rationale: A fair test changes only one thing. A clean dark card each time shows exactly how much dust landed. Drilling once without the shroud and once with it, on the same model block for the same time, shows what the shroud catches, because the shroud is the only change. Without the clean card, old dust would mix into the new reading.

title: Stand behind the rope with the crew lead
instruction: Stand behind the rope at the edge of the work area with the crew lead.
rationale: A building site is busy, with tools running and people carrying heavy things. Standing behind the rope keeps the class clear of the crew's work and out of their way. The crew lead watches the site so the class can watch the lesson. Watching from the rope also gives the best view of the whole site at once.

title: Set the drill timer and leave it
instruction: Turn the timer dial to the teacher's setting for both runs.
rationale: Both runs must last the same time, or the test is not fair. A longer run would leave more dust on the card whatever else happened. Setting the timer once for both runs keeps the time the same, so only the shroud changes. Scientists call this keeping everything else the same.

title: Read the dust on the card
instruction: Commit when the marker matches the card's colour on the grey scale.
rationale: Matching the card against a grey scale turns what you see into a reading you can compare. A grey card means more dust landed, and a dark clean card means less. Real dust monitors on building sites do the same job much more precisely, and they can measure dust far too fine to see.

title: Hold the model drill square to the block
instruction: Hold the model drill flat against the block until the timer ends.
rationale: The shroud only catches dust when it sits flat on the surface. If the drill tips, a gap opens and dust escapes past the shroud. Holding it square is the same skill the real crew uses, and it is what makes the test honest. A steady hand matters more than a fast one here.

title: Move the bench to where the breeze comes from
instruction: Drag the model bench to the side of the work area the breeze blows from.
rationale: No dust catcher is perfect, and the breeze carries whatever escapes. Working on the side the breeze comes from sends that little bit of dust away from you instead of into your face. Builders choose where to stand for the same reason. Watching the flag or a strip of tape on a fence shows which way the breeze is blowing.

title: Spot how the crew protects their breathing
instruction: Look across the site and mark each thing the crew does for clean air.
rationale: The national rule for silica dust on building sites asks builders to catch dust at many tools with water or a vacuum, and to clean up without dry sweeping or blowing. When a job still makes dust, the crew's written plan can ask for a fitted mask too. Each of these keeps the air clean where people work, and the plan on the board says which one goes with which tool.

title: Say what your cards showed
instruction: Choose the sentence that says what the two runs showed.
rationale: Both runs lasted the same time on the same block with clean cards. The card from the run without the shroud came out greyer, and the card from the run with the shroud stayed darker. A good answer says the shroud caught much of the dust, and it does not claim more than the two cards showed.

title: Follow the dust puff on the breeze
instruction: Keep the marker on the dust puff as the breeze carries it across the site.
rationale: Dust does not stay where it is made. A breeze carries it across the site to people who are not even drilling. Following the puff shows why one crew's dust is everyone's business, and why builders catch it at the drill instead of hoping it blows away.

title: Record the crew's dust plan in your own words
instruction: Write the ways the crew keeps dust out of the air, and name where you learned them.
rationale: Writing the plan in your own words shows you understood it, and naming the source shows where it came from. A careful scientist or reporter always says where a fact came from, so someone else can check it. Your record can list the shroud, the water, the vacuum and the place to stand, each in one short line.

title: Share one way to keep dust out of the air
instruction: Tell another group one way builders stop drilling dust from reaching people.
rationale: Workers, neighbours and visitors all share the air around a building site. Sharing ways to catch dust helps the class see that small habits, like using a vacuum instead of a brush, keep the air clean for everyone. Hearing another group's way often reminds you of one you forgot.

title: Check in before leaving the site
instruction: How does the crew catch drilling dust? Why does it matter where you stand?
rationale: The crew talks over each visit before the class leaves the site. Each learner names a way to catch dust and says why the breeze matters. If anyone thinks the dust is just dirt, the group sorts it out now. Then everyone leaves knowing the same few habits.

situation: The little vacuum hose slips off the model drill's shroud and a puff of dust appears.
instruction: Stop the model drill first, then fix the hose.
missed: The model drill kept running while the hose hung loose, and a little cloud settled on the bench.

situation: Dust from another crew's work drifts toward the class on the breeze.
instruction: Step aside out of the dust's path with the crew lead, who asks the other crew to stop.
missed: The class stayed in the dust's path until the crew lead moved everyone aside, upwind of the drill.

explanation: You went to blow the dust off the card. Blowing lifts the finest dust into the air, where people breathe it. Builders use a special vacuum to pick dust up instead, and the class does the same with the little vacuum.

You said concrete dust is just dirt. Concrete has sand and stone in it, and drilling grinds some of that into dust finer than you can see. That fine dust is why builders catch it at the drill instead of letting it float around.
You picked up a dry brush to sweep the bench. A dry brush throws fine dust back into the air. Builders use a vacuum or a damp cloth, so the dust ends up in the bag and not in anyone's breath.
You started toward the crew's real drill. The crew is working, and visitors watch from behind the rope with the crew lead. Everything the class needs to see is on the model bench.

title: Find the simple machines in the crane
instruction: Mark the three simple machines in the model crane.
rationale: A crane is several simple machines working together. The boom is a lever turning about its pivot, the hook block is a set of pulleys, and the winch drum is a wheel and axle. Finding each one in the model shows that the big machines on the quay are built from ideas you can test on a bench.

title: Know the rule: never under a load
instruction: Read the card: never stand or reach under a suspended load.
rationale: A suspended load can slip, swing or drop, and the space beneath it is the most dangerous place near any crane. The rule applies to the bench model too, because the habit you practise here is the one that keeps people safe on every quay and building site.

title: Put the pulley test in order
instruction: Weigh the pull with one line, add lines, weigh again, then measure the rope pulled.
rationale: Measuring the pull with one line first gives a baseline to compare with. Adding lines and measuring again shows the pull getting smaller, and measuring the length of rope you had to pull shows where the trade happens: less force, more distance, and never less work.

title: Hold the force meter steady on the rope
instruction: Hold the force meter still on the rope while the load hangs clear.
rationale: A force meter only reads the pull correctly while the load is hanging still; any jerk or swing adds to the reading. Holding it steady until the needle settles gives a number you can compare fairly with the next test.

title: Say why more pulleys make pulling easier
instruction: Say why more pulley lines make the pull easier, and what you give up.
rationale: More lines share the load, so each carries less and your pull is smaller, but you must pull a longer length of rope. Saying both halves, easier pull and longer rope, is understanding the trade instead of thinking the machine gives something for nothing.

title: Spot the problems in a classmate's explanation
instruction: Look at the draft explanation and mark each problem.
rationale: Explanations of machines go wrong in the same ways: a machine said to give free work, a longer reach said to lift more and a load chart called a rough guide. Spotting them helps you write explanations that are true as well as tidy.

title: Turn the winch handle to lift the load
instruction: Turn the winch handle and watch how far it turns for a small lift.
rationale: The handle travels round a big circle while the drum winds only a little rope, which is how a small push on the handle lifts a heavy load. Feeling how many turns a short lift takes is the wheel and axle's trade, felt in your own hand.

title: Read the pull at the right moment
instruction: Commit when the force meter shows the steady pull with the load held still.
rationale: The pull needed to hold a load still is the fair measurement; the pull while starting or speeding up is larger. Reading at the steady moment is what lets you compare one line with several and see the pulleys' effect clearly.

title: Move the load closer on the model boom
instruction: Drag the load block to the reach where the model's load chart allows it.
rationale: The same load has a bigger turning effect the further out it hangs, so a crane can lift less at long reach. Moving it inside the chart's limit is exactly the decision an operator makes before every lift, with the chart, not a guess, as the guide.

title: Lower the load smoothly
instruction: Keep the lowering speed steady as the model load comes down.
rationale: Lowering smoothly keeps the load from swinging and stops sudden jerks that load the rope far more than the steady weight does. Operators lower with care for the same reason, and feeling it on the model shows why speed changes matter.

title: Record the test results
instruction: Write the pull and the rope length for each number of lines.
rationale: A results table puts force and distance side by side, so the trade becomes visible: as one goes down the other goes up. Writing both for each test is what turns a demonstration into evidence someone else can check.

title: Ask the operator how they use the chart
instruction: Ask the crane operator how the load chart guides a real lift.
rationale: Hearing an operator explain how they check reach, load and configuration before every lift connects the science to a skilled trade. It shows that the ideas tested on the bench are the ones professionals rely on every shift.

title: Check in at the end of the session
